hook.en: A giant whose name is a poets' word for the sea; at his ale-feast Loki insults the gods.

value.en: A giant in Hymiskviða; for Snorri a man from Hlésey skilled in magic, who visited Ásgarðr and heard Bragi tell the gods' stories. Also called Hlér and Gymir; 'ægir' is also a poets' word for the sea.
His wife is Rán; they have nine daughters, whose names poets use in phrases for the sea
Feasting the gods. Þórr orders him to brew for them; he demands a kettle big enough, which Þórr fetches from Hymir. At his feasts gleaming gold lights the hall and the ale serves itself.
Loki kills his servant Fimafengr, and at the end of Lokasenna curses his hall to burn

why.en: Ægir comes to Ásgarðr, where swords light the hall.
The giant's revenge: bring me a kettle big enough.
The feast in his hall where Lokasenna happens.
Loki's parting curse on Ægir and his hall.

hook.en: A place in heaven where the light-elves live, fairer to look upon than the sun; the gods gave it to Freyr.

value.en: One of the glorious places in heaven (Snorri)
The light-elves, fairer than the sun; unlike the dark-elves, who live down in the earth and are blacker than pitch
Grímnismál: the gods gave Álfheimr to Freyr "as a tooth-gift" in days of old

why.en: Light-elves and dark-elves compared.
Freyr's tooth-gift.

hook.en: The second of the sun's two horses, driven by Sól across the sky with bellows to cool him.

value.en: One of the two horses of the sun, with Árvakr; Sól, daughter of Mundilfari, drives them
The gods set wind-bags under their shoulders to cool them
Sigrdrífumál says runes were cut on Alsviðr's hoof (there spelled Alsvinnr)
Skáldskaparmál's list of horse names, which repeats that Árvakr and Alsviðr draw the sun

why.en: How Sól came to drive the sun's horses.
The sun's horses in Óðinn's verse.

hook.en: A dwarf who came to claim Þórr's daughter, and was kept answering questions until daylight caught him.

value.en: A dwarf; his name means "all-wise" in Old Norse. Þórr says he is pale round the nose, as if he had lain with the dead, and looks like a giant.
Under the earth; his home is beneath a stone
Coming to take home a bride promised while Þórr was away. Þórr, her father, refuses unless the dwarf can tell him everything he asks.
Telling what things are called among men, gods, giants, elves and dwarves. The dwarves, for example, call the sun Dvalins leika, "Dvalinn's playmate" (the English has "The Deceiver of Dvalin").
Þórr ends the contest: "The day has caught thee, dwarf!" The sun shines into the hall. The poem does not say what happens to him then.

why.en: The dwarf introduces himself and his home under the stone.
A sample answer: the sun's names in six worlds.
The last stanza: Þórr's trick is revealed at sunrise.

hook.en: The ring Loki tore from the dwarf Andvari, cursed to be the death of whoever owns it.

value.en: "Andvari's Yield": the one gold ring Andvari tried to hide when Loki took his hoard. He said he could make wealth grow from it.
Andvari's curse: it would be the death of everyone who owned it. Loki passed the curse on, and Snorri says it came true.
Óðinn wanted it for himself, but had to use it to cover the last whisker of the otter-skin paid to Hreiðmarr
Sigurðr, in Gunnarr's shape, gave it to Brynhildr as a bride-gift. In the queens' quarrel Guðrún names the ring and says Gunnarr never won it. After Sigurðr's death Gunnarr and Högni took it.
In Dráp Niflunga, Guðrún sends it to Högni with a wolf's hair tied in it, as a warning not to go to Atli

why.en: Andvari loses the ring and lays the curse.
Guðrún reveals the truth by naming the ring.
The ring as a silent warning with a wolf's hair.

hook.en: A dwarf who lived as a pike in a waterfall, lost all his gold to Loki, and cursed it.

value.en: A dwarf, son of Óinn. He says an evil norn doomed him to live in water. He is also in the dwarf lists of Völuspá and Snorri.
A waterfall, Andvari's falls, where he lived in the shape of a pike; Snorri says he was "a fish in the water" in the land of the black elves and kept his gold in a rock
All his gold, to pay for the killing of Otr. Snorri says Loki caught him with his hands; in Reginsmál Loki borrows Rán's net. He tried to keep back one ring, and Loki took that too.
His curse: the ring would be the death of whoever owned it. In Reginsmál the gold will bring death to two brothers and strife to eight princes.

why.en: The pike speaks: Andvari names himself and his fate.
Snorri's version: the hidden ring and the curse.
The curse in verse, foretelling the deaths to come.

hook.en: A giantess of Jötunheimar who bore Loki three children the gods feared: a wolf, a serpent and Hel.

value.en: A giantess (gýgr) living in Jötunheimar
With Loki: Fenrir, Jörmungandr and Hel, in Snorri. Völuspá in skamma names only the wolf
Prophecies warned the gods of great harm from her children: bad from the mother's side, worse from the father's

why.en: Loki's three monstrous children, and why the gods sent for them.
A short verse: Loki's wolf by Angrboða, and Sleipnir by Svaðilfari.

hook.en: “Early-Wake”, one of the two horses that pull the sun's chariot, cooled by bellows set under their shoulders.

value.en: One of the two horses of the sun, with Alsviðr. The gods set Sól, daughter of Mundilfari, to drive them
The gods set two wind-bags under their shoulders to cool them; some records call this ísarnkol, “iron-coolness”
Sigrdrífumál says runes were cut on Árvakr's ear
Skáldskaparmál's list of horse names, which repeats that Árvakr and Alsviðr draw the sun

why.en: Mundilfari's proud children and the sun's horses.
The sun's horses in Óðinn's verse.
Places where runes were carved, Árvakr's ear among them.

hook.en: The gods' stronghold in the middle of the world; Snorri adds that "men call it Troy".

value.en: The stronghold the sons of Borr built for themselves "in the middle of the world", where the gods and their kin lived
Snorri says "men call it Troy"; he also speaks of an Elder Ásgarðr (Ásgarðr inn forni), where Allfather had twelve names
The gods. From the seat Hliðskjálf there Óðinn saw over all worlds and every man's deeds
Iðavöllr lies in the middle of it; there the gods built Glaðsheimr and Vingólf
Loki warns in Þrymskviða that without Þórr's hammer the giants will soon settle in Ásgarðr
After Ragnarök the surviving gods live on Iðavöllr, "where Ásgard was before"

why.en: Snorri builds Ásgarðr — and links it to Troy.
King Gylfi travels to Ásgarðr in disguise.

hook.en: The first cow, formed from dripping rime, who fed Ymir with four rivers of milk and licked Búri out of the ice.

value.en: A cow that came into being from the dripping rime at the beginning of the world; she appears only in Snorri
Four rivers of milk ran from her udders, and she fed the giant Ymir
She fed by licking the salty ice-blocks. Over three days a man came out: first hair, then a head, then the whole man, Búri
Búri's son Borr married the giant's daughter Bestla, and their sons were Óðinn, Vili and Vé
Auðhumla, the spelling of this text

why.en: The cow appears and feeds Ymir.
Three days of licking, and the gods' ancestor emerges.

hook.en: A dwarf set under a corner of the sky; at the world's end, a skald says, "The Toil of Austri bursteth".

value.en: One of four dwarves the gods set under the four corners of the sky: Austri, Vestri, Norðri, Suðri (East, West, North, South)
Under a corner of the sky, which the gods made from the skull of the giant Ymir
Poets may call the sky the "helm" of Vestri, Austri, Suðri and Norðri, or the "task" or "burden" of the dwarves
A skald pictures the end of the world: the sun goes dark, the earth sinks, and "the toil of Austri" (the sky) bursts
The name also stands in Völuspá's list of dwarves

why.en: The gods build the sky from Ymir's skull.
How poets name the sky after the four dwarves.
Arnórr's verse: the sky Austri holds breaks apart.

hook.en: The best and brightest of the gods, killed by a shaft of mistletoe, who returns when the world rises new.

value.en: Son of Óðinn and Frigg. His wife is Nanna, daughter of Nep; their son is Forseti.
The best of the gods, praised by all; so fair and bright that light shines from him. He is the wisest and most gracious of the Æsir, yet none of his judgments can stand.
Breiðablik, in heaven, a place where nothing unclean may be.
He owns the ship Hringhorni, greatest of all ships, which became his funeral pyre, and the ring Draupnir, which Óðinn laid on that pyre.
His death. He has dreams of danger; Frigg makes all things swear not to harm him, but skips the young mistletoe. Blind Höðr shoots it at Loki's prompting and kills him.
Hel will let him go only if every thing in the world weeps for him; one giantess, Þökk, refuses. After Ragnarök he and Höðr come back from Hel to the renewed world.

why.en: Snorri's portrait: so bright that light shines from him.
The dead seeress names Höðr as Baldr's killer.
Frigg lets slip that the mistletoe swore no oath.
Hel's terms: every thing must weep for him.
Baldr comes back in the new world.

hook.en: Suttungr's brother, who hired a stranger called Bölverkr for a summer and helped him drill into a mountain.

value.en: Brother of Suttungr.
His nine thralls kill each other with their scythes, fighting over a whetstone thrown by Óðinn.
He hires "Bölverkr" (Óðinn) to do nine men's work for a summer, for the wage of one drink of Suttungr's mead.
He drills into the mountain with the auger Rati, lies that he is through, and stabs after Óðinn when he slips in as a snake — and misses.

why.en: A giant short of farmhands meets Bölverkr.
The drilling, and Baugi's double-cross.

hook.en: The one Freyr killed with a hart's horn, because he had already given away his sword.

value.en: Killed by Freyr, who fought him without his sword and used a hart's horn. The texts never say what kind of being Beli was.
Snorri's Hárr says it was no great matter: Freyr could have killed him with his bare hand. The sword will be missed far more at Ragnarök.
Poets name Freyr after him: "Beli's fair slayer" in Völuspá, "Adversary of Beli" in Skáldskaparmál.

why.en: The fight with an antler.
"Beli's fair slayer" seeks out Surtr at Ragnarök.

hook.en: The one frost giant who survived the flood of Ymir's blood — the oldest thing the wise Vafþrúðnir can remember.

value.en: A frost giant born countless winters before the earth was made.
Son of Þrúðgelmir and grandson of Aurgelmir, whom Snorri identifies with Ymir.
When Ymir was killed he escaped the blood-flood with his wife and household on his "lúðr"; the later frost giants descend from them.
Vafþrúðnir's earliest memory is of Bergelmir being laid on a lúðr. In Snorri he climbs onto it and survives the flood, so it seems to be a vessel; the poem does not explain the word.

why.en: Snorri's flood story: the only survivor and his wife.
The giant's oldest memory, quoted by Snorri too.
His family line back to Aurgelmir.

hook.en: The gods' bridge from earth to heaven — the rainbow, Snorri suggests, with fire burning in its red.

value.en: A bridge the gods made from earth to heaven; "it may be that ye call it rainbow". It has three colours and is very strong
Ásbrú, "the Æsir's Bridge"; Bilröst in the poems
The red in it is burning fire, which keeps the frost-giants and hill-giants from walking up into heaven
Heimdallr, at Himinbjörg by its end, guards it against the hill-giants
It will break when the sons of Múspell ride over it at Ragnarök

why.en: Hárr laughs at the question: you must have seen it.
Why the gods are not to blame for a breakable bridge.
The bridge burns with flame; Þórr must wade instead.

hook.en: Þórr's hall, with 540 rooms: the biggest house anyone knows of.

value.en: Þórr's hall, in his realm Þrúðvangar
540 rooms; "the greatest house that men know of". In Grímnismál Óðinn calls it the biggest roofed house he knows: "my son's"
Þórr; in poetry he can be called "Possessor" of Bilskirnir

why.en: Óðinn counts the rooms of his son's hall.
Snorri introduces Þórr and his house.

hook.en: One of the vats that held Kvasir's blood; Óðinn emptied it with his second draught.

value.en: One of two vats (with Són) that, with the kettle Óðrerir, took Kvasir's blood when Fjalarr and Galarr killed him
Óðinn emptied Boðn with his second draught in Hnitbjörg
Poetry is called the liquid "of Bodn"; a skald begins "Now that which Bodn's Billow / Bodes forth will straight be uttered".

why.en: The three vessels are named.
A skald calls his poem Boðn's wave.

hook.en: Sigmundr's queen from Brálundr: mother of Helgi, and the woman who poisoned her stepson Sinfjötli.

value.en: Sigmundr Völsungsson; he lived long in her kingdom in Denmark
Helgi, born in Brálundr
Sinfjötli killed her brother in a quarrel over a woman. She had to accept Sigmundr's compensation, but at the funeral feast she brought Sinfjötli poison three times, until he drank and died

why.en: Helgi's birth in Brálundr: "Borghild's son".
The three horns of poison.

hook.en: Father of Óðinn, Vili and Vé, known almost only through "the sons of Borr", who killed Ymir and built the world.

value.en: Búri, the man the cow Auðhumla licked out of the salty ice blocks over three days.
Bestla, daughter of the giant Bölþorn.
Óðinn, Vili and Vé.
His sons kill Ymir, make the earth, sea and sky from him, and shape the first humans from two trees. In Völuspá "Burr's sons" raise the land and make Miðgarðr.
The text does not call Borr a giant: Búri is "fair of feature, great and mighty". It is his wife who is a giant's daughter.

why.en: The family tree of the gods begins here.
The sons of Burr lift the land.
Borr's sons make the first man and woman.

hook.en: The god of poetry and Iðunn's husband; Snorri says the very word for poetry, bragr, comes from his name.

value.en: Wisdom and above all eloquence and skill with words. Poetry is called bragr after him; Snorri calls him the first maker of poetry, and the long-bearded god.
Iðunn, who keeps the apples that make the gods young again
Óðinn, in Snorri's list of ways to name him
At Ægir's feast he sits next to Ægir and tells him the gods' stories, which frame Snorri's Skáldskaparmál
In Lokasenna he offers Loki a horse, a sword and a ring to keep the peace; Loki calls him the least brave of all

why.en: Snorri introduces him and explains the word bragr.
Bragi beside Ægir: the storytelling that frames Skáldskaparmál begins.
Loki's sharpest insult: Bragi is shyest of the shot.
Of all skalds, Bragi is named the best.
In a quoted verse Óðinn sends Hermóðr and Bragi to greet a dead king.

hook.en: Baldr's hall in heaven, where nothing unclean may be — the land with the fewest baleful runes.

value.en: Baldr's dwelling, in heaven; "there is not in heaven a fairer dwelling"
Baldr, Óðinn's second son
Nothing unclean may be there; it lies in the land with the "fewest baneful runes"

why.en: Breiðablik in Grímnismál's list of halls.
Snorri's portrait of Baldr and his home.

hook.en: Freyja's necklace: it bursts when she snorts with rage, then is put on Þórr when he is disguised as a bride.

value.en: Freyja ("Freyja átti Brísingamen").
When Loki and Þórr ask Freyja to marry the giant Þrymr, she snorts so angrily that the gods' hall shakes and the necklace bursts
Heimdallr proposes dressing Þórr as the bride with "the mighty Brisings' necklace", and so it is done

Snorri knows another tale: Heimdallr fought Loki over the necklace at Vágasker and Singasteinn, told in Úlfr Uggason's Húsdrápa, where both were in the shape of seals. Loki is called "Thief ... of Brísinga-men".

why.en: Freyja's fury bursts the necklace.
Þórr dressed as a bride, necklace and all.
Traces of a lost myth: Heimdallr and Loki fight for it.

hook.en: A dwarf who won a bet for Loki's head, could not take it, and sewed Loki's lips shut instead.

value.en: His brother is the smith Sindri

Working the bellows while Sindri forged a gold-bristled boar, the ring Draupnir and a hammer. A fly stung him each time; the third time he let go of the bellows for a moment, and Sindri said everything had nearly been spoiled. The hammer's handle turned out rather short.
Giving the treasures: the ring to Óðinn, the boar to Freyr, the hammer to Þórr. The gods judged the hammer best, so he won the bet.
Claiming Loki's head. Loki said the head was his but not the neck, so Brokkr sewed Loki's lips together; the thong is called Vartari.

why.en: The forging scene: three treasures, a stinging fly, a near disaster.
Brokkr presents the gifts and says what each one can do.
How the bet ends: Loki's neck and Loki's lips.

hook.en: A valkyrie who vowed to marry only the man who rode through fire — and was tricked into marrying the wrong one.

value.en: A valkyrie. In Snorri the armoured woman Sigurðr wakes on the mountain names herself Hildr and "is called Brynhildr"; Sigrdrífumál calls that woman Sigrdrífa; in Helreið Brynhildar Brynhildr tells that story as her own
Daughter of Buðli; sister of Atli; fostered by Heimir
She vowed to marry only the man who dared ride through the fire round her hall. Sigurðr rode it in Gunnarr's shape and laid his sword between them in bed
Gunnarr, son of Gjúki. Of Sigurðr she says: "His wife is Guthrun, and Gunnar's am I"
Told the truth by Guðrún at the river, she drove Gunnarr to have Sigurðr killed, then stabbed herself and was burned near him; on her way to Hel a giantess blocks her road

why.en: The quarrel over whose husband is braver, washing hair in the river.
She laughs once, with all her heart, at Guðrún's wailing.
A giantess tries to stop her on the road to Hel.
She asks for the sword to lie between them again on the pyre.

hook.en: A king known almost only as a father: of Atli, of Brynhildr, and of the house of the Buðlungar.

value.en: Atli and Brynhildr; poems call Brynhildr "Buðli's daughter" again and again
His hall passed to Atli: in Atlamál the Gjúkungs come to "the home that Buðli once had"; in Atlakviða the burning hall is the house of the Buðlungar
In Sigurðarkviða in skamma Brynhildr's servants burned with Sigurðr were Buðli's gifts to his daughter
Atli remembers that there were five brothers "when we lost Buðli"

why.en: Grípir first names Brynhildr as Buðli's daughter.
Atli counts his dead brothers.

hook.en: Day, the bright son of Night and Dellingr; his horse's shining mane lights all the sky and earth.

value.en: Son of Nótt (Night) and Dellingr; bright and fair like his father. Brother of Auðr and Jörð (Earth).
Skinfaxi, whose mane lights all the air and the earth
Óðinn set him and his mother in the sky with horses and chariots to ride round the earth

why.en: Day's birth and his ride round the earth.
Óðinn names the horse that draws the day.
"The father of Day is Dellingr called."

hook.en: A god of the Æsir's kin, Night's third husband and father of Day; a dwarf once sang a spell before his doors.

value.en: One of the race of the Æsir
Third husband of Nótt (Night) and father of Dagr (Day), who is bright and fair like him
In Hávamál the dwarf Þjóðrerir sang a spell of strength for the gods before Dellingr's doors

why.en: The giant names the fathers of Day and Night.
A dwarf's spell sung before Dellingr's doors.

hook.en: Snorri's dark-elves live down in the earth and are "blacker than pitch"; whether they are dwarves is left open.

value.en: Down in the earth
Being blacker than pitch, unlike the light-elves in looks and far more unlike in nature

Snorri never says they are dwarves. But his dwarves also live in the earth and stones, and the land of the black elves (Svartálfaheimr) is where Loki finds the dwarf Andvari and Skírnir finds the dwarves who make Gleipnir.
Loki swears to get the black elves to make Sif's golden hair, and then goes to the dwarves called Ívaldi's sons
The late poem Forspjallsljóð names dwarfs and dökkálfar ("Murk Alfs" in the English) side by side among those going to rest under the world-tree's root.

why.en: The only description of the dark-elves in Snorri.
Black elves promised, dwarves delivered: read it closely.
A late poem lists dwarfs and dark-elves together.

hook.en: A gold ring that drips eight more of equal weight every ninth night.

value.en: Forged by the dwarf Sindri while Brokkr worked the bellows; Brokkr gave it to Óðinn
Every ninth night eight gold rings of the same weight drip from it
Óðinn laid it on Baldr's pyre. In Hel, Baldr gave it to Hermóðr to take back to Óðinn as a keepsake.
In Skírnismál, Skírnir offers Gerðr "the ring that was burned / Of old with Othin's son", from which eight of like weight fall every ninth night; the poem does not name it.
Poets call gold "Draupnir's Drop" and "Shower of Draupnir", and Baldr "Possessor of Hringhorni and Draupnir". A dwarf in Völuspá's list is also called Draupnir.

why.en: Brokkr hands Óðinn the ring and says what it does.
Baldr sends the ring back from Hel.
The same kind of ring offered to win Gerðr.

hook.en: The second, much stronger fetter for Fenrir; the wolf risked it for fame and shook it to pieces.

value.en: The Æsir's second fetter for the wolf, "stronger by half" than Læðingr
The gods told the wolf he would be famous if it could not hold him. He decided he must take risks to win fame, let them bind him, and broke it so that the pieces flew far.
A proverb: "to dash out of Drómi" is said when anything is exceeding hard.
Named with Læðingr in Eddubrot as the two fetters that failed

why.en: The wolf weighs the risk and breaks Drómi.
Eddubrot's short account names both failed fetters.

hook.en: The second of the dwarves in Völuspá, after Móðsognir, the greatest of them all.

value.en: A dwarf, named second after Móðsognir, the greatest of them
"They made many in man's likeness, dwarves in the earth, as Durinn said"
In Snorri, the dwarves first came alive as maggots in the flesh of the giant Ymir; the gods gave them human shape and understanding
Like all dwarves in Snorri, he lives in the earth and in stones

why.en: The seeress names the first two dwarves.
Snorri explains where dwarves came from.

hook.en: A dwarf who cut runes for the dwarves, as Óðinn did for the gods; some norns are called his daughters.

value.en: A dwarf named early in Völuspá's list; part of the list is the race of the dwarfs "in Dvalin's throng".
Cutting runes for the dwarves, as Óðinn did for the gods and Dáinn for the elves
Some norns are "Dvalinn's daughters"; others are of god-kin or elf-kin
Poets call the sun "Dvalinn's Playmate" and poetry the "Drink of Dvalinn".
Also one of four harts that feed in the branches of Yggdrasill; and in Hervararkviða a sword is the one "which Dvalinn forged"

why.en: Óðinn names who cut runes for each race.
Fáfnir on the norns and their mixed descent.
The other Dvalinn: a hart gnawing the world-tree.

hook.en: A hart standing on Valhöll whose antlers drip so much that all the world's waters flow from it.

value.en: He stands on Valhöll and bites the branches of the tree Læraðr
So much drips from his horns that it runs down into Hvergelmir, and from there all the rivers run
Snorri and Grímnismál name the rivers: Síð, Víð, Sækin, Ekin and many more; some flow round the gods' dwellings, some fall down to Hel

why.en: Eikþyrnir in Óðinn's description of Valhöll.
Snorri's account, with the long list of rivers.

hook.en: Snorri says just one thing about the third goddess: she is the best of physicians.

value.en: The third of the Ásynjur in Snorri's list of goddesses
"She is the best physician"
In Fjölsvinnsmál, one of the maidens who sit at Menglöð's knees is named Eir. These maidens help people who make offerings to them. The poem does not say whether she is the same Eir.

why.en: Snorri's entire account of Eir, in two short sentences.
The maidens at Menglöð's knees, Eir among them.

hook.en: The brother who offered as much help as one foot gives the other, and was killed for it on the road.

value.en: In Snorri, son of Guðrún and Jónakr, full brother of Sörli and Hamðir, raven-haired like the Niflungs. In Hamðismál he is a half-brother, of another mother (sundrmæðri), and they call him a bastard
Asked what help he would give, he said: as much as hand gives foot (Snorri), or as one foot gives the other (Hamðismál)
His brothers killed him on the way; Snorri says they did it to hurt their mother, because she loved him most
Too late, Hamðir says Jörmunrekkr's head would be off "if Erpr lived"
Not to be confused with Erpr son of Atli and Guðrún, whom Guðrún killed with his brother Eitill

why.en: His answer, and the brothers' scorn.
Erpr's one line from horseback.
Sörli stumbles and understands.

hook.en: Brynhildr's brother and Guðrún's second husband, who killed her brothers for their gold and unknowingly ate his own sons.

value.en: Son of Buðli; brother of Brynhildr and Oddrún. In Atlamál he says there were five brothers when Buðli died
Guðrún, after Sigurðr's death; their sons were Erpr and Eitill
Inviting Gunnarr and Högni to his court, capturing them, cutting out Högni's heart and throwing Gunnarr to the snakes
His sons: Guðrún gave him their skulls as drinking cups, their blood in his drink and their hearts to eat
Told by his concubine Herkja that Guðrún lay with Þjóðrekr; Guðrún cleared herself by drawing stones from a boiling kettle, and Herkja's hands were burned
Killed by Guðrún: with Högni's son as he slept, in Snorri; with Högni's son, in Atlamál; with her sword in his bed, in Atlakviða. Snorri and Atlakviða add the burning of his hall

why.en: Guðrún tells him what he has eaten.
His dreams foretell it: plants torn up, red with blood.
Dying, he reproaches her for betraying one who trusted her.

hook.en: A man who killed his father for gold, then lay on it in serpent shape, wearing a helmet every creature feared.

value.en: Son of Hreiðmarr; brother of Reginn and Otr
Killing his father for the gold paid for Otr: with Reginn, in Snorri; alone, stabbing him in his sleep, in Reginsmál
The "helm of terror" (ægishjálmr), which all living things fear, and the sword Hrotti
Gnitaheiðr, where he turned into a serpent and lay on the gold; his lair had iron doors and iron beams, dug into the earth
Sigurðr dug a pit across the track he used to crawl to water and stabbed him from below

why.en: "Youth, oh, youth!" — the dying serpent questions his killer.
He warns that the gold and rings will be Sigurðr's death.
He warns Sigurðr: "Regin betrayed me, and thee will betray."

hook.en: A giant, the father of Loki — almost the only thing the Eddas tell of him.

value.en: Loki, whose mother is Laufey or Nál; Loki's brothers are Býleistr and Helblindi
A giant
His son's name in poetry: Snorri lists "son of Fárbauti" for Loki, and Úlfr Uggason calls Loki "Fárbauti's sin-sly offspring" in the fight at Singasteinn, where Heimdallr strove with Loki

why.en: Snorri's account of Loki's parents and brothers.
A skald's verse naming Loki as Fárbauti's son.

hook.en: A giantess enslaved to turn a magic mill, who ground out an army against the king who allowed her no rest.

value.en: Giant-born and "fore-knowing". She and Menja say they are born of the giants Iði and Aurnir, and boast of Hrungnir and Þjazi as mighty.
King Fróði of Denmark buys her and Menja from King Fjölnir of Sweden because they are big and strong.
They turn the mill Grótti, which grinds whatever is asked: gold, peace and happiness for Fróði. He lets them rest only as long as a cuckoo is silent.
They grind an army: the sea-king Mýsingr kills Fróði and takes the mill and the women. He makes them grind salt until his ship sinks — and so the sea is salt.
In their song they recall nine winters under the earth, when they moved a mountain from its place, and later fighting in Sweden.
Poets call gold "Fenja's Labor".

why.en: The mill and the cruel king.
The slave women name their giant kin.
Why the sea is salt.

hook.en: Loki's wolf-son, raised by the gods, tricked into a silken fetter, and fated to swallow Óðinn at Ragnarök.

value.en: Son of Loki and the giantess Angrboða; brother of Jörmungandr and Hel
The gods raised him at home and only Týr dared feed him. He broke the fetters Læðingr and Drómi; the dwarf-made band Gleipnir held him
He let Gleipnir be put on him only if a god laid a hand in his mouth as a pledge. When the gods would not free him, he bit off Týr's right hand
Fenrisúlfr; Vánargandr, the "Monster of Ván" (Ván is the river of slaver that runs from his gagged mouth); in Lokasenna Týr calls him Hróðrsvitnir
None named for certain. Völuspá says an old giantess in Járnviðr bore "the brood of Fenrir"; Grímnismál calls the wolf Hati son of Hróðvitnir, a name Týr uses for Fenrir in Lokasenna.
At Ragnarök he breaks loose and swallows Óðinn. Víðarr kills him by tearing his jaws apart (Snorri, Vafþrúðnismál); in Völuspá Víðarr thrusts a sword to his heart

why.en: The binding: Týr's hand in the wolf's mouth, and a sword as gag.
The wolf's own words: he smells a trick and demands a pledge.
Týr answers Loki: each has lost something to the wolf's binding.
Ragnarök: the wolf swallows Óðinn and Víðarr avenges him.
After “fenrir” takes the sun, her daughter will ride her paths.

hook.en: Frigg's hall, where she wept for Valhöll and where Loki, disguised as a woman, drew out her secret.

value.en: Frigg's dwelling, "most glorious"
Loki came there in a woman's shape; Frigg told him that she had taken oaths from weapons and trees not to harm Baldr
In Völuspá, Frigg weeps in Fensalir "For Valhall's need"
Frigg; in poetry she can be called "Mistress" of Fensalir

why.en: Loki's visit in disguise.
Frigg's tears in Fensalir.

hook.en: A dwarf who, with his brother Galarr, murdered the wise Kvasir and brewed the mead of poetry from his blood.

value.en: This card is the dwarf of Skáldskaparmál. The name also belongs to a red cock that crows before Ragnarök, and in Hárbarðsljóð to someone Hárbarðr says Þórr was too scared to sneeze near while he hid in a glove. A dwarf Fjalarr stands in Völuspá's dwarf list.
He and Galarr kill Kvasir, run his blood into two vats and a kettle, and mix it with honey. Whoever drinks becomes a poet or scholar. They tell the gods Kvasir choked on his own wisdom.
They drown the giant Gillingr, and Fjalarr has Galarr drop a millstone on his wailing widow.
The mead, paid to Gillingr's son Suttungr as ransom for their lives.
In Hávamál the speaker says he was dead drunk "with Fjalar wise"; which Fjalarr is meant is not said.

why.en: The murder of Kvasir.
The dwarves' second and third killings.
Marooned on a skerry, they give up the mead.

hook.en: The surly gatekeeper of Menglöð's hall, who answers the stranger's every question but bars the gate to all but Svipdagr.

value.en: The warden at the gate. The stranger takes him for an ogre; he calls himself wise of mind but mean with food.
He names what the stranger sees: Menglöð who rules the hall, the gate Þrymgjöll, the hounds Gífr and Geri, the tree Mímameiðr, and Lævateinn, made by Loptr and kept by Sinmara.
He says he built the enclosure Gastrópnir himself, from the limbs of Leirbrimir.
Only Svipdagr may sleep in Menglöð's arms, he says. When the stranger names himself Svipdagr, Fjölsviðr calls Menglöð to see him.
Fjölsviðr ("very wise") is also one of Óðinn's names; the poem does not say the gatekeeper is Óðinn.

why.en: The gatekeeper turns the stranger away.
A wall made from a giant's limbs.
The gate opens and the hounds fawn.

hook.en: Baldr's son, who settles every dispute brought to his gold-and-silver hall Glitnir.

value.en: Son of Baldr and Nanna, daughter of Nepr
Glitnir, a hall in heaven with pillars of gold and a roof of silver
All who bring him a quarrel go away reconciled; his is the best court among gods and men
One of the twelve Æsir who sit as judges at the feast for Ægir

why.en: Snorri's whole account of him.
Glitnir described: gold pillars, silver roof, all strife laid to rest.
He takes his seat among the twelve judging Æsir.

hook.en: Óðinn's second wolf, fed from his table, and an old poetic word for any wolf: “the Greedy One”.

value.en: One of Óðinn's two wolves; the other is Geri
Óðinn gives them the food set on his table, since he lives on wine alone
His name, "Greedy One", is also a poets' word for any wolf, as in a verse by Egill
Völuspá's refrain uses “freki” for the wolf that will run free when the fetter breaks

why.en: Óðinn feeds Geri and Freki.
Snorri lists the poets' words for wolf.

hook.en: The goddess of love whom giants keep demanding as their price; she weeps tears of red gold for a missing husband.

value.en: Daughter of Njörðr, sister of Freyr; wife of Óðr and mother of Hnoss
Her husband Óðr went away on long journeys. She weeps for him and her tears are red gold; searching for him among unknown peoples, she took many names: Mardöll, Hörn, Gefn, Sýr.
Fólkvangr, with her great hall Sessrúmnir. Each day she chooses half of the slain; Óðinn has the other half.
The necklace Brísingamen, which burst when she snorted with rage in Þrymskviða; and a falcon or feather shape, which she lends to Loki

A chariot drawn by two cats. In Hyndluljóð a golden-bristled boar, Hildisvíni, made by the dwarves Dáinn and Nabbi, goes with her. The giantess Hyndla claims her lover Óttarr rides with her; Freyja answers that it is only her boar.
Giants keep asking for her: the builder of the gods' wall wants her as his pay, Þrymr will return Þórr's hammer only for her, and the drunk Hrungnir means to take her home

why.en: Told to marry a giant, her fury bursts her necklace.
Snorri's portrait: Óðr, Hnoss, golden tears and many names.
Loki accuses her before all the gods.
Freyja wakes the giantess Hyndla to ride with her to Valhöll.
Fólkvangr, and her half of the slain.

hook.en: God of rain, sun and harvest, who gave away his sword to win a giantess, and lacks it at the end.

value.en: Rain, sunshine and the fruits of the earth. People call on him for good seasons, peace and wealth.
Son of Njörðr, brother of Freyja; husband of the giantess Gerðr
Álfheimr, which the gods gave him long ago as a tooth-gift
The ship Skíðblaðnir, made by the sons of Ívaldi: all the Æsir fit aboard, yet it folds up into a pouch. And the boar Gullinbursti, which runs over sky and sea and pulls his chariot.
His sword, which fights by itself. He gave it to his servant Skírnir as the price for wooing Gerðr, so later he fought Beli without a weapon and killed him with a hart's antler.
At Ragnarök he fights Surtr and falls, because he lacks the sword he gave away

why.en: Freyr sits in Óðinn's seat and sees Gerðr light up the world.
Lovesick Freyr: one night is long, how can he wait three?
Týr defends him: he makes no woman weep and frees the bound.
Loki's taunt: he bought Gymir's daughter with gold and his sword.
"Beli's fair slayer" goes out against Surtr.

hook.en: Óðinn's wife knows every fate but never tells it. She took an oath from everything to spare Baldr, except one young sprout.

value.en: Óðinn's wife and the foremost of the goddesses. Her maids Fulla and Gná serve her, and she owns a hawk-plumage that Loki once borrowed. Poets call her "Lady of the Æsir and Ásynjur".
Daughter of Fjörgynn, mother of Baldr, and mother-in-law of Nanna
Fensalir, a "most glorious" estate
She knows the fates of men but makes no prophecies. Freyja says the same in Lokasenna.
She made fire, water, metals, stones, sicknesses, beasts and poisons swear not to harm Baldr. She skipped the mistletoe as too young, and she let this slip to Loki, who was disguised as a woman.
Völuspá calls her Hlín. When Óðinn goes to fight the wolf at Ragnarök, she suffers "another hurt", a second grief. Her first was Baldr's death, when she wept in Fensalir.

why.en: Frigg's fatal slip: the mistletoe seemed too young to swear.
After Baldr dies, she asks who will ride to Hel to ransom him.
Frigg and Óðinn wager over a king; her warning gets Óðinn seized and tortured.
She tries to keep Óðinn at home, away from the wise giant.
Loki accuses her about Vili and Vé. Her answer recalls Baldr.

hook.en: Frigg's maid and keeper of her secrets. She carries her mistress's box and looks after her shoes.

value.en: The fifth goddess in Snorri's list. She is a maiden who wears her hair loose with a gold band around her head.
She carries Frigg's box, looks after her shoes and shares her secret plans. Poets call Frigg "mistress of Fulla".
In the prose of Grímnismál, Frigg sends her to warn King Geirröðr against a "magician". The magician is the disguised Óðinn, and the king tortures him.
After Baldr's death, Nanna sends her a gold finger-ring from Hel
In poetry, gold is called "Snood of Fulla" or "Fulla's Snood": her headband

why.en: The only description of her: loose hair, gold band, Frigg's secrets.
Fulla's warning to the king sets the whole of Grímnismál in motion.

hook.en: The dwarf who, at his brother's word, dropped a millstone on a drowned giant's weeping wife.

value.en: A dwarf, brother of Fjalarr
With Fjalarr, killing the wise Kvasir and making the mead of poetry from his blood and honey
Waiting above the door and dropping a millstone on the head of Gillingr's wife, after the brothers had drowned Gillingr
The mead, given to Suttungr to be let off the tidal reef alive. So poetry is called "Dwarves' Drink" and "Ferry-Boat of Dwarves".

why.en: Fjalarr's whispered order and Galarr's millstone.
Suttungr's revenge, and why poetry is the dwarves' ship.

hook.en: The best of hounds, bound before the cave Gnipahellir; his howling marks the coming of Ragnarök.

value.en: A hound: “of hounds Garmr” is the best, as Sleipnir is of horses
Bound before Gnipahellir; Snorri calls him “the greatest monster”
Völuspá's refrain: “Now Garm howls loud before Gnipahellir”; the fetter will break and the wolf run free
Loose at Ragnarök, he fights Týr, and each kills the other
In Baldrs draumar Óðinn meets a hound coming from Hel, bloody on the breast; the poem does not name it

why.en: The seeress's refrain, repeated as the end draws near.
Garmr and Týr kill each other in the last battle.
The list of the best: tree, ship, god, horse, hound.

hook.en: She ploughed a piece of Sweden loose with four oxen, who were her own giant-born sons, and dragged it out to sea.

value.en: A woman of the Æsir. King Gylfi gave her, as a wandering woman, as much land as four oxen could plough in a day and a night.
She yoked four oxen from Jötunheimar, her sons by a giant. They tore the land loose and dragged it west, and she named it Zealand (Selund). The hole they left became a lake in Sweden.
The fourth goddess in Snorri's list. There he calls her a maiden and says that women who die unmarried serve her, though in chapter 1 she has four sons.
In Lokasenna she tries to stop the quarrel. Loki claims a fair youth gave her a necklace and she lay with him. Óðinn warns that she knows all fates as well as he does.

why.en: The opening of Gylfaginning: how Zealand was ploughed out of Sweden.
Bragi's old verse on Gefjun's oxen, sweating as they plough.
Óðinn defends her: she sees fate as clearly as he does.

hook.en: A giant who caught Loki in falcon shape and starved him until he promised to bring Þórr without his hammer.

value.en: A giant whom the giantess Gríðr calls "a crafty giant and ill to deal with". Not the King Geirröðr of Grímnismál, who is a human king.
He catches Loki, who was flying in Frigg's falcon shape, locks him in a chest for three months, and lets him go on an oath to bring Þórr without hammer or belt of strength.
The giantesses Gjálp and Greip.
He throws a glowing lump of iron at Þórr; Þórr catches it in iron gloves and throws it back through an iron pillar, through Geirröðr and through the wall.
Poets call Þórr his slayer (ON vegandi Geirröðar; the English has "Smiter of Hrungnir, of Geirrödr").

why.en: Loki is caught peeping through a window.
The chair that rises toward the roof.
The glowing iron flies back.

hook.en: A giant's daughter whose raised arms lit up sea and sky; Freyr saw her once and could not sleep or drink.

value.en: Daughter of Gymir and of Aurboða, who was of the hill-giants' kin; the most beautiful of all women
When she lifted her hands to open a door, light shone from her arms over sky and sea, and all the worlds grew bright
Freyr. She refuses Skírnir's golden apples and the ring, and gives way only to threats of the sword and a curse of runes. She promises to meet Freyr in the grove Barri after nine nights.
She fears the stranger at her door may be "my brother's slayer"; the brother is never named
Snorri counts her among the goddesses seated at the Æsir's feast

why.en: Freyr describes the girl whose arms lit up the sky.
Her answer to the bribe: no lack of gold in Gymir's house.
She gives in, offering the frost-cup of old mead.
Her promise: the grove Barri, nine nights from now.

hook.en: One of Óðinn's two wolves, who eat the food from his table, since Óðinn himself lives on wine alone.

value.en: One of Óðinn's two wolves; the other is Freki
Óðinn gives them the food set on his table; he needs none, for wine is both food and drink to him
His name is also a poets' word for any wolf
A different Geri, with Gífr, is one of two hounds guarding a gate in Fjölsvinnsmál, a later poem outside the Codex Regius

why.en: Óðinn feeds his wolves and lives on wine.
Snorri's answer: does Óðinn eat what his warriors eat?

hook.en: A hall fairer than the sun, roofed with gold, that still stands when heaven and earth are gone.

value.en: A hall at the southern end of heaven, brighter than the sun and roofed with gold
Good and righteous people, for all ages
It will stand when both heaven and earth have passed away; after Ragnarök it is the best place to be
Snorri thinks it lies in a third heaven, Víðbláinn, above a second called Andlangr; only light-elves live there now

why.en: The seeress sees a hall roofed with gold.
Good and evil halls after the end.

hook.en: The yawning gap before the world: ice from the north, sparks from the south, and mild air where they met.

value.en: The emptiness at the beginning, "when nothing was": no sand, sea or earth, "a yawning gap, and grass nowhere"
Its north filled with ice and rime, its south was lit by sparks from Múspell; the middle was "mild as windless air", and there Ymir came alive
The sons of Borr carried Ymir into the middle of it and made the earth from his body
Later the root of Yggdrasill among the frost-giants stands where Ginnungagap once was

why.en: The beginning, in Völuspá's words.
Ice meets heat and life begins.

hook.en: Heimdallr's horn: its blast is heard in all worlds, and it will wake the gods for the last battle.

value.en: The horn of Heimdallr, the gods' watchman; its blast is heard in all worlds
When Ragnarök begins, Heimdallr blows it hard and wakes all the gods to hold council
Snorri also says Mímir drinks from his well out of the Gjallarhorn

why.en: Heimdallr, his senses, and his horn.
"Loud blows Heimdall, the horn is aloft."
The horn at Mímir's well.

hook.en: Geirröðr's daughter, who stood astride a river and swelled it to drown Þórr — until he threw a stone.

value.en: Daughter of the giant Geirröðr; sister of Greip.
She stands with a foot on each side of the river Vimur and makes it rise to Þórr's shoulders. He throws a stone at her: "At its source should a river be stemmed."
She and Greip were under Þórr's chair as it rose toward the roof; he pushes back with Gríðr's staff and breaks both their backs. A skald praises Þórr: "Didst stand on lifeless Gjálp".
Völuspá in skamma names a Gjálp among the nine giantesses who bore Heimdallr; it may be another figure.

why.en: The giantess in the gorge.
Under the chair.
Þórr's own verse about Gjálp and Greip.

hook.en: A king known through his children: Gunnarr, Högni and Guðrún, whose quarrels with Sigurðr and Atli end his line.

value.en: Wife Grímhildr; children Gunnarr, Högni, Guðrún and Guðný; Gotthormr was his stepson
A sister, Gjaflaug, who tells Guðrún of losing five husbands
Giving Guðrún, with gold, to Sigurðr
His sons are called the Gjúkungar, also the Niflungar; so gold is called "Treasure, or Heritage, of the Niflungs"
His line ends with Sörli and Hamðir: then "all the house and offspring of Gjúki were dead"

why.en: Sigurðr arrives at Gjúki's court and marries his daughter.
Atlamál ends praising the children Gjúki fathered.

hook.en: The gods' first court: a hall all of gold, with twelve seats and Allfather's high seat.

value.en: The temple (hof) holding the gods' twelve seats and Allfather's high seat; "the best-made of any on earth", like one piece of gold inside and out
On Iðavöllr, in the middle of Ásgarðr
In Grímnismál it is the fifth dwelling, where gold-bright Valhöll stands wide

why.en: The first thing the gods built.
Glaðsheimr and Valhöll in Óðinn's list of halls.

hook.en: The fetter that holds the wolf Fenrir: soft as silk, made from things like a cat's footfall and a woman's beard.

value.en: Made by dwarves in the land of the black elves, after Óðinn sent Freyr's servant Skírnir to them
Made of the noise of a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, the roots of a mountain, a bear's sinews, a fish's breath and a bird's spittle. The Eddubrot verse has "the milk of birds" instead of spittle.
Hárr's proof: "a woman has no beard", a cat's leap makes no sound, a rock has no roots
Smooth and soft as a silk ribbon. The wolf would not let it on him without a god's hand in his mouth; Týr gave his, and the harder the wolf fought, the tighter the band grew.
At Ragnarök all fetters break and Fenrir gets loose

why.en: The six impossible ingredients.
Gleipnir holds; Týr loses his hand.
The recipe in verse, slightly different.

hook.en: Forseti's hall of gold and silver, where every quarrel ends in reconciliation.

value.en: A hall whose walls, posts and pillars are of red gold and whose roof is silver
Forseti, son of Baldr and Nanna
Everyone who comes there with a dispute leaves reconciled: "the best seat of judgment among gods and men"

why.en: Glitnir in Grímnismál: Forseti settles all strife.
Snorri on Forseti's court.

hook.en: Frigg's messenger rides a horse across sky and sea. When the Vanir asked what was flying, she said she does not fly.

value.en: The fourteenth of the Ásynjur. Frigg sends her into various worlds on her errands.
Hófvarpnir, a horse that runs over sky and sea. Its sire is Hamskerpir and its dam is Garðrofa.
Some of the Vanir once saw her riding in the air and asked what flew there. She answered in verse: she does not fly, though she fares and glides on Hófvarpnir.
Snorri says that from her name, something that rises high is said to gnæfa (to tower)

why.en: The Vanir's question, in verse.
Gná's answer, with her horse's pedigree.

hook.en: The cave where the hound Garmr is bound; his howling there is the refrain of Völuspá's end.

value.en: The dog Garmr is bound in front of it, "the greatest monster"
Völuspá's refrain, repeated four times: "Now Garm howls loud before Gnipahellir, the fetters will burst"
At Ragnarök Garmr breaks loose and fights Týr; each kills the other

why.en: The first time the refrain sounds.
Garmr loose at Ragnarök, against Týr.

hook.en: One of two valkyries sent by Óðinn to bring a fallen king home to Valhöll.

value.en: A valkyrie named in Völuspá's list of "Herjan's maidens" ready to ride
With Skögul, sent by Óðinn "to choose from kings who of Yngvi's kin should go with Odin and be in Valhall"
Snorri: Óðinn sends the valkyries to every battle; they choose who is to die and decide the victory
Poets build battle-names on hers: "the Clash of Göndul", and glymvindr Göndlar, Göndul's crashing storm-wind.

why.en: The opening of Eyvindr's poem on a king's death.
Göndul in the oldest list of valkyries.
A battle-kenning built on her name.

hook.en: Sigurðr's horse, who carried Fáfnir's gold and hung his head to the grass when his master was killed.

value.en: Sigurðr's horse, chosen from King Hjálprekr's stud
Fáfnir's hoard, so gold is called “Grani's burden”
He would carry no one but Sigurðr, so Sigurðr rode him through the fire to Brynhildr in Gunnarr's shape
After Sigurðr's death Grani came running back without him, and bowed his head to the grass when Guðrún spoke to him

why.en: Grani will not carry Gunnarr through the flames.
Guðrún questions the grieving horse.

hook.en: Geirröðr's other daughter, who with her sister Gjálp lifted Þórr's chair toward the roof — and died under it.

value.en: Daughter of the giant Geirröðr; sister of Gjálp.
Under the chair in the goat-shed she and Gjálp lift Þórr toward the rafters; he pushes back with Gríðr's staff and breaks both their backs.
Þórr recalls in verse how "Gjálp and Greip" tried to lift him to the sky.
Völuspá in skamma names a Greip among the nine giantess mothers of Heimdallr; it may be another figure.

why.en: The crash and the scream under the chair.
Þórr's verse about the two sisters.

hook.en: The queen whose drink made Guðrún forget her murdered husband and agree to marry Atli.

value.en: King Gjúki; mother of Gunnarr, Högni and Guðrún
Grípir foretells that her wiles will trap Sigurðr: she offers him her daughter and gets him to woo Brynhildr for Gunnarr
She gave Guðrún a cold, bitter drink mixed with "magic earth", ice-cold sea and swine's blood, so she forgot Sigurðr's killing; then pressed her to marry Atli
A queen; Guðrúnarkviða II calls her "the Gothic queen" (gotnesk kona)
In Atlamál Guðrún accuses Atli of having murdered her mother for treasure

why.en: The forgetting-drink, ingredient by ingredient.
Marry Atli, or stay without a husband for life.

hook.en: A magic mill that ground out whatever was asked: gold and peace for a king, then an army against him.

value.en: Two millstones found in Denmark, too heavy for anyone to turn; they ground out whatever the grinder asked for. Hengikjöptr gave them to King Fróði.
Fróði bought two huge, strong slave-women, Fenja and Menja, and made them grind gold, peace and happiness with almost no rest
Singing, they ground out an army: the sea-king Mýsingr came that night, killed Fróði and took the mill. So ended Fróði's peace.
Snorri: on Mýsingr's ship they ground salt until the ship sank; the sea has been salt ever since. In Gróttasöngr the poem ends instead with the heavy stone bursting in two.
The maidens sing that Grótti would not have come out of the grey mountain if they had known nothing of it; the line is obscure.

why.en: The maidens grind gold and peace for Fróði.
The army, the salt, and the sinking ship.
The giant-maidens break the mill.

hook.en: Married three times, she outlived every husband and child, and fed Atli the hearts of their own sons.

value.en: Daughter of Gjúki and Grímhildr; sister of Gunnarr, Högni and Guðný
First Sigurðr; then Atli, whom she married against her will after Grímhildr's drink of forgetting; then King Jónakr. "Three hearths I knew"
With Sigurðr: Sigmundr and Svanhildr. With Atli: two sons, named Erpr and Eitill in the poems. With Jónakr: Sörli, Hamðir and Erpr

Avenging her brothers on Atli: she killed their sons, served him their hearts and their blood, then killed him. Snorri and Atlakviða add that she burned the hall; in Atlamál she gives him a ship and a coffin instead
She walked into the sea to die, but the waves carried her to Jónakr's land; later she sent her sons to avenge Svanhildr

why.en: After a whole poem of silence, she finally weeps.
The cold, bitter drink that made her forget.
She lifts stones from a boiling kettle to prove her innocence.
She takes up a sword and fights beside her brothers.
"Three hearths I knew" — her life summed up by herself.

hook.en: Freyr's boar with bristles of gold, forged by a dwarf, which runs through air and sea and lights up the dark.

value.en: A boar belonging to Freyr; also called Slíðrugtanni, “Fearful-Tusk”
Loki wagered his head that the dwarf Sindri could not match the gods' treasures. Sindri laid a pigskin in the forge, and his brother Brokkr kept the bellows going though a fly stung him
Brokkr gave it to Freyr: it runs through air and sea faster than any horse, and its bristles give light in the darkest night
Freyr drives in his chariot with this boar to Baldr's funeral
In Hyndluljóð it is Freyja's boar Hildisvíni that is “gullinbursti”, golden-bristled, made by the dwarfs Dáinn and Nabbi

why.en: The smithing contest: a fly, a pigskin and a golden boar.
Brokkr hands over the treasures and says what each can do.
Freyja's golden-bristled boar, made by other dwarfs.

hook.en: Heimdallr's horse “Gold-top”, one of the steeds the gods ride each day to their court at the well of Urðr.

value.en: The horse of Heimdallr
Named among the horses the Æsir ride each day over Bifröst to hold court at Urðr's well
Heimdallr rides him to Baldr's funeral
A skald's list of famous horses

why.en: Heimdallr's portrait: golden teeth, horse, horn and keen ears.
Who came to Baldr's funeral, and on what.
The gods' horses, named in verse.

hook.en: A woman the gods speared and burned three times in Óðinn's hall; three times she was reborn, and she lives still.

value.en: A woman named only once, in Völuspá; the poem does not say where she came from. The next stanza tells of a seeress called Heiðr; many readers take her to be Gullveig, but the poem does not say so.
She is pierced with spears and burned in the hall of Hárr (Óðinn), three times; three times she is born again, and she still lives
The seeress links her burning to the war, "the first in the world", in which Óðinn throws his spear, the gods' wall is broken and the Vanir take the field

why.en: The whole of what is told of her, in ten short lines.
Heiðr the seeress, perhaps the same woman.
The war breaks out: Óðinn's spear, the broken wall.

hook.en: Óðinn's spear, made by Ívaldi's sons; once thrust, it never stops.

value.en: Made by the dwarves called Ívaldi's sons, together with Sif's golden hair and the ship Skíðblaðnir, at Loki's request
Loki gave it to Óðinn, saying the spear would never stop in its thrust
At Ragnarök Óðinn rides first with his gold helmet and Gungnir against the wolf Fenrir
Runes were cut "On Gungnir's point", says Sigrdrífumál; a skald says "Hroptr bore with him Gungnir" (Hroptr is Óðinn).

why.en: The gods judge the treasures; Óðinn gets the spear.
Óðinn rides out with Gungnir to his last fight.
Gungnir among the places where runes were cut.

hook.en: He could not ride through fire, and died in a snake pit playing a harp — some say with his toes.

value.en: Son of Gjúki and Grímhildr; brother of Högni and Guðrún; sworn brother of Sigurðr
Goti, the horse that "dared not leap into the fire" round Brynhildr's hall
Brynhildr; later Glaumvör. He sought Atli's sister Oddrún, who loved him, but Atli would take no bride-price from him
Before riding to Atli he and Högni sank Fáfnir's gold in the Rhine; Snorri says it "has never since been found". In Atlakviða he will not tell where it is until shown Högni's heart

Atli had him thrown into a snake pit. He played a harp — with his toes in Snorri and Atlamál, with his hand in Atlakviða. An adder bit him to the liver (Snorri); in Oddrúnargrátr it is Atli's mother who digs into his heart

why.en: He knows Högni's heart because it does not tremble.
He plays so well the women weep and the rafters burst.
After the killing, Gunnarr alone lies awake long into the night.

hook.en: The giantess set to guard the mead of poetry, who gave Óðinn three drinks after three nights — and was left weeping.

value.en: Daughter of the giant Suttungr.
She guards the mead inside Hnitbjörg.
"Bölverkr" lies with her three nights; she lets him drink three times, and he empties Óðrerir, Boðn and Són.
In Hávamál Óðinn says she gave him the mead on a golden chair, that he could hardly have escaped without her, and that he repaid her badly. The poem adds that he left her in grief.
Poets can call the earth "rival of Frigg, Rindr and Gunnlöð", counting her among Óðinn's women.

why.en: Three nights, three drinks.
Óðinn's memory of the golden chair.
Óðinn admits he owed his escape to her.
The speaker lay drunk, "fettered", "in Gunnloth's house".

hook.en: The giant whose house held Gerðr — and so much gold that his daughter scorned the gifts Freyr sent.

value.en: Husband of Aurboða, who was of the hill-giants' kin; father of Gerðr
Gymir's courts in the land of giants, with fierce dogs tied at the gate and flickering fire around them
Wealth and temper: Gerðr says there is no lack of gold in his house and that he will gladly fight Skírnir; Skírnir answers that the old giant is doomed
Not the same as Ægir, though the Lokasenna prose and Snorri also call Ægir Gymir

why.en: His daughter's boast about her father's gold.
Skírnir's threat: the old giant will die by this sword.
Loki: Freyr bought Gymir's daughter with gold.

hook.en: Óðinn's bench-mate and travelling companion, who gave the first humans their sense and was handed to the Vanir as a hostage.

value.en: In Völuspá three gods bring Askr and Embla to life: Óðinn gives breath, Hœnir gives sense (óðr), Lóðurr gives warmth and colour. Snorri instead gives this to the sons of Borr.
When the Æsir and Vanir made peace, the Vanir gave Njörðr as a hostage and took Hœnir in exchange
Óðinn's bench-mate, companion and friend; the swift god; Long-Foot; King of Clay
He travels with Óðinn and Loki: when Þjazi steals their meal, and when Loki kills the otter
After Ragnarök he chooses the lot-wood in the renewed world

why.en: Breath, sense, warmth: the three gifts that made humans alive.
The hostage exchange that ended the war of gods and Vanir.
Three gods on the road — the start of the Þjazi story.
One of the few gods with a role in the new world.

hook.en: Guðrún's son, sent to avenge his sister; no iron could bite him, so his enemies used stones.

value.en: Son of Guðrún and King Jónakr; brother of Sörli and Erpr; Svanhildr was their sister
He answered his mother's taunts bitterly: she would have had small praise for Högni's deed when Sigurðr was woken from sleep and killed, and she had killed her own sons by Atli
Mail-coats and helmets from his mother, so strong that iron would not bite them
On the way he and Sörli killed their brother Erpr. At Jörmunrekkr's hall they cut off the king's hands and feet; Hamðir said his head would be off too "if Erpr lived"
Jörmunrekkr told his men to stone them, since weapons would not bite; Sörli fell by the gable, Hamðir at the back of the house

why.en: Hamðir regrets killing Erpr: "His head were now off".
Sörli's last words for both: "We have greatly fought", whatever the Norns decree.
He foretells his own death to his mother.

hook.en: The wolf who runs ahead of the sun, eager to seize the moon, called the son of Hróðvitnir.

value.en: In Snorri, the wolf who runs before the sun and wants to take the moon, “and so it must be”
Hróðvitnir, in both Snorri and Grímnismál. In Lokasenna Týr uses the name Hróðrsvitnir for Loki's bound wolf, Fenrir
Snorri makes the sun- and moon-wolves the brood of an old giantess in Járnviðr; Völuspá calls that brood "the brood of Fenrir"
Grímnismál links him with the sun rather than the moon: he goes before “the burning bride of heaven”
At Ragnarök “the other wolf” seizes the moon; Snorri does not name it there

why.en: Hati Hróðvitnisson, running ahead of the sun.
Óðinn names Sköll and Hati, son of Hróðvitnir.
Týr's reply to Loki uses the same wolf-name, Hróðrsvitnir.

hook.en: A she-goat on the roof of Valhöll whose udders give enough mead each day to make every warrior drunk.

value.en: She stands on Valhöll and bites the branches of the tree Læraðr
Mead runs from her udders and fills a great vat every day, enough for all the einherjar to drink their fill
Snorri's answer to whether the warriors drink water: All-father (Óðinn) would never give kings and earls water
In Hyndluljóð the giantess Hyndla taunts Freyja that she runs out at night like Heiðrún among the he-goats

why.en: What the dead warriors drink.
Heiðrún in Óðinn's own description of Valhöll.

hook.en: The gods' watchman at the end of the rainbow bridge, who hears grass grow and will sound the horn at Ragnarök.

value.en: Watchman of the gods, called the White God. He sits at heaven's end guarding the bridge against the hill-giants. He needs less sleep than a bird, sees a hundred leagues by night or day, and hears grass and wool grow.
Nine maidens, all sisters, bore him as their son. Snorri also calls him a son of Óðinn.
Himinbjörg, at heaven's end where Bifröst reaches the sky; there he drinks good mead in his snug hall
The horn Gjallarhorn, whose blast is heard in all worlds.
His horse Gulltoppr
Hallinskíði and Gullintanni (his teeth were of gold), and Vindlér; in the prose before Rígsþula he travels among men calling himself Rígr
At Ragnarök he blows Gjallarhorn to wake the gods; then he and Loki kill each other

why.en: Snorri's full portrait: nine mothers, golden teeth, ears that hear grass grow.
The seeress addresses all humankind as "Heimdall's sons".
He fought Loki for Freyja's necklace, both in the shape of seals.
His idea: dress Þórr as a bride to win back the hammer.
Loki mocks him: forever on watch, with a muddy back.

hook.en: Loki's daughter, half dark and half flesh-coloured, whom Óðinn sent below to rule those who die of sickness or old age.

value.en: Ruler of the dead, and also the name of her realm: Snorri says evil men go to Hel and thence to Niflhel
Daughter of Loki and the giantess Angrboða; sister of Fenrir and Jörmungandr
Óðinn cast her into Niflheimr and gave her power over nine worlds. Her hall is Éljúðnir; her dish Hunger, her knife Famine. Grímnismál puts Hel under one root of Yggdrasill
Her looks: “half blue-black and half flesh-color”, grim and fierce
She will release Baldr only if everything in the world weeps for him. A giantess who calls herself Þökk refuses: "Let Hel hold to that she hath!"
At Ragnarök all Hel's people (Heljarsinnar) follow Loki to the last battle

why.en: Snorri's portrait of Hel, her hall, her servants and her bed.
Hel's condition for letting Baldr go home.
Þökk's dry tears: the one refusal that keeps Baldr below.
Óðinn rides up to Hel's high hall to question a dead seeress.

hook.en: A silent, nameless boy until a valkyrie named him; dying, he asked his bride to love his brother instead.

value.en: Son of King Hjörvarðr and Sigrlinn, daughter of King Sváfnir; Heðinn, son of another of Hjörvarðr's wives, was his brother
The valkyrie Sváfa gave him his name and told him of a sword at Sigarshólmr, with a blood-flecked snake on the blade
With his companion Atli he killed Hróðmarr, avenging his mother's father, and killed the giant Hati; Atli kept Hati's daughter Hrímgerðr talking until daybreak turned her to stone
Sváfa, daughter of King Eylimi; they exchanged vows, and she stayed with her father, still a valkyrie
Mortally wounded in a duel with Álfr, son of Hróðmarr, he asked Sváfa to take his brother Heðinn instead; she refused

why.en: The valkyrie rouses the nameless, silent boy.
Hrímgerðr caught by daylight: "in stone thou shalt ever stand".
Sváfa's refusal: no unknown prince in her arms.

hook.en: Born while eagles screamed, he killed King Hundingr at fifteen and came back from Valhöll for one night with Sigrún.

value.en: Son of Sigmundr and Borghildr, born in Brálundr; named after Helgi Hjörvarðsson; fostered by Hagall
Killing King Hundingr (at fifteen, in the first lay) and then his sons; hence the name "Hundingsbani", Hundingr's slayer
Sigrún, daughter of King Högni. Her father had promised her to Höðbroddr; Helgi fought Granmarr's sons for her and killed her father Högni and her brother Bragi
Sigrún's brother Dagr, after a sacrifice to Óðinn, borrowed Óðinn's spear and killed him at Fjöturlundr
In Valhöll Óðinn offered him rule over everything with himself; he rode back to his burial mound, where Sigrún spent a night with him
He and Sigrún were said to be born again as Helgi Haddingjaskati and Kára — "now called old wives' folly"

why.en: His birth: eagles screaming, holy streams falling from the heavens.
Sigrún: he stood above heroes like an ash above thorns.
In Valhöll he sets his old enemy Hundingr to menial work.
Sigrún kisses the dead king, his hair heavy with frost.

hook.en: The god who rode Sleipnir nine nights down to Hel to bring Baldr home — and very nearly did.

value.en: Hermóðr the Bold, a son of Óðinn, who takes up Frigg's call for someone to ride to Hel and ransom Baldr
Óðinn's horse Sleipnir: nine nights through dark, deep valleys to the river Gjöll and its gold-roofed bridge
The bridge-keeper says the bridge thunders no less under him alone than under five troops of the dead, and that he lacks a dead man's colour
He leaps Sleipnir over Hel's gate, finds his brother Baldr in the high seat, and wins Hel's terms: Baldr returns if all things weep for him
Home again: the ring Draupnir, sent by Baldr to Óðinn, and Nanna's gifts for Frigg
In poetry a Hermóðr is given helmet and mail-coat by Óðinn, and with Bragi greets a dead king; whether this is the same figure is unclear

why.en: Frigg asks for a volunteer, and Hermóðr mounts Sleipnir.
At the bridge to Hel: "thou hast not the color of dead men".
The leap over Hel-gate and a night with Baldr.
Hel's condition: all things, living and dead, must weep.

hook.en: A valkyrie's name worn by three women: an ale-bearer in Valhöll, Brynhildr, and a princess who raises the dead.

value.en: A valkyrie in Völuspá's list of "Herjan's maidens" ready to ride, and in Grímnismál among those who bring ale to the einherjar
Snorri: Óðinn sends the valkyries to every battle; they choose who is to die and decide the victory
When Sigurðr cut the mail-coat from a sleeping woman, she "gave her name as Hildr: she is called Brynhildr"
Hildr, King Högni's daughter, carried off by Heðinn: she offered her father a necklace for peace, then each night woke the dead by magic, so the battle goes on until Ragnarök

why.en: The valkyries gather, Hildr among them.
Sigurðr wakes the valkyrie who calls herself Hildr.
Hildr raises the dead every night: a battle without end.

hook.en: Heimdallr's house at heaven's end, by the head of the bridge Bifröst, where the watchman drinks good mead.

value.en: At heaven's end, at the bridge-head where Bifröst comes to heaven
Heimdallr, the gods' watchman, guarding the bridge against the hill-giants
In Grímnismál the eighth dwelling: Heimdallr rules the holy places there and gladly drinks good mead

why.en: Heimdallr: hears grass grow, guards the bridge.
The watchman's mead at Himinbjörg.

hook.en: Sigurðr's mother: daughter of King Eylimi, wife of Sigmundr after Borghildr, and later of Álfr.

value.en: Daughter of King Eylimi; sister of the far-seeing Grípir
Sigmundr, in Frankland; after he fell in battle she married Álfr, son of King Hjálprekr, and Sigurðr grew up there
Sigurðr, who names her when he introduces himself

why.en: "Sigurth am I, and Sigmund's son, and Hjordis..."
Her marriages, briefly.

hook.en: A high seat from which one sees all the worlds; Freyr's pride in sitting there cost him his peace.

value.en: In Ásgarðr; in another chapter Snorri puts it in Valaskjálf, Óðinn's hall thatched with silver
When Óðinn sits there he sees all the worlds and what every man is doing
Freyr sat in it, saw Gerðr in Jötunheimar and fell sick with love; Snorri calls this a punishment for his pride in sitting in the holy seat
Óðinn and Frigg sit there watching their foster-sons; later Óðinn spots the hiding Loki from it

why.en: Óðinn's view over the whole world.
Freyr looks north and loses his heart.
Óðinn and Frigg watch, and wager, from the seat.

hook.en: Freyja's daughter, so beautiful that precious things are called "hnossir" after her.

value.en: Freyja
Óðr
Her beauty: things that are fair and precious are called hnossir after her name. A skald calls a precious gift "Hörn's Child"; Hörn is one of Freyja's names.

why.en: Snorri's one sentence on her, inside Freyja's portrait.
Freyja named "mother of Hnoss" in a skald's verse.

hook.en: Blind and weaponless, he shot a sprig of mistletoe where Loki pointed — and Baldr fell dead.

value.en: A blind god, and strong. The gods would rather never have to name him, for his deed will long be remembered.
Óðinn
Killing Baldr. He stood outside the ring because he was blind; Loki told him to shoot the mistletoe and showed him where, and the shot went through Baldr.
Baldrs draumar has the seeress foretell that Höðr will bear the fatal branch; Völuspá tells how he shot it.
Váli kills him in revenge for Baldr
After Ragnarök he and Baldr come back from Hel and live together in the renewed world

why.en: His only words: he cannot see Baldr and has no weapon.
The shot itself, "the greatest mischance" among gods and men.
The dead seeress names him as Baldr's slayer before it happens.
Höðr and Baldr together again in the new world.

hook.en: Gunnarr's brother, who laughed while they cut the heart out of his living body.

value.en: Son of Gjúki; brother of Gunnarr and Guðrún
Kostbera, who read Guðrún's warning runes and dreamed of disaster. Atlamál names their sons Snævarr and Sólarr; a son of Högni helps Guðrún kill Atli
In Sigurðarkviða in skamma he refuses to break the oaths sworn to Sigurðr, so Gunnarr turns to their younger brother Gotthormr; Snorri says both brothers were urged on and both turned to Gotthormr
He read the ring Guðrún sent, wound with a wolf's hair, as a warning not to go
Atli had his heart cut out while he lived, and he laughed. In Atlakviða the thrall Hjalli's heart is cut out first, to fool Gunnarr; in Atlamál Högni begs for the thrall's life

why.en: "Then Högni laughed" — the heart-cutting.
He begs for the cowardly cook's life.
He will not break the oaths sworn to Sigurðr.

hook.en: A giant in eagle's shape at the edge of heaven: when he spreads his wings, the wind blows over the world.

value.en: A giant (jötunn) in the shape of an eagle; not the unnamed eagle that sits in Yggdrasill
He sits at the end of heaven; Snorri says the northern end
The winds come from under his wings when he takes flight
Óðinn asks where the wind comes from in his wisdom contest with the giant Vafþrúðnir, and this is the answer

why.en: Vafþrúðnir explains the wind.
Snorri's answer, then the same verse quoted.

hook.en: A farmer skilled in magic who seized three gods and made them pay for his son's death in gold.

value.en: A powerful householder, "very skilled in black magic", who gave the travelling gods a night's lodging
Sons Fáfnir, Reginn and Otr; daughters Lyngheiðr and Lofnheiðr
Binding Óðinn, Loki and Hœnir and demanding that Otr's skin be filled and covered with red gold; he spotted one uncovered whisker, and Óðinn covered it with Andvari's ring

He refused his sons any share and was killed for the gold: by both sons in Snorri, by Fáfnir alone as he slept in Reginsmál. Dying, he called on his daughters, telling one to bear a daughter whose son might avenge him

why.en: The whisker: Hreiðmarr inspects the gold-covered skin closely.
"Gifts ye gave, but ye gave not kindly."
Dying, he calls his daughters; their answer is cold.

hook.en: “Frosty-Mane”, the horse that draws Night across the sky; the foam from his bit falls as the morning dew.

value.en: The horse of Nótt (Night). All-father gave Nótt and her son Dagr each a horse and chariot to ride round the earth
Each morning he bedews the earth with foam from his bit; Vafþrúðnismál says that is where the dew in the valleys comes from
Óðinn names him in his wisdom contest with Vafþrúðnir as the horse that brings night from the east
Fjörsvartnir

why.en: Night, Day and their two horses.
Óðinn's answer about the horse of night.

hook.en: A giantess who tried to wreck Helgi's fleet, traded insults with his watchman all night, and was turned to stone at dawn.

value.en: Daughter of the giant Hati, whom Helgi killed. Her mother also lay in wait for the ships.
A long war of insults with Helgi's watchman Atli: he calls her a corpse-greedy witch, she calls him a gelding.
She asks to sleep one night with Helgi as compensation for her father. Helgi tells her the giant Lóðinn is a fitter mate.
She reveals that the fleet was guarded by three times nine maidens, led by a white maiden in a helmet.
Atli keeps her talking until daylight; she turns to stone and stands as a harbour mark for men to laugh at.

why.en: She names herself and her father.
Her bold demand of Helgi.
The riders who saved the ships.
Daybreak.

hook.en: Baldr's ship, greatest of all ships, which no god could launch for his funeral.

value.en: Baldr. It is the greatest of all ships.
The gods wanted to build Baldr's pyre on it but could not move it. The giantess Hyrrokkin pushed it out at the first shove, so that fire flew from the rollers and the lands shook.
Baldr's body was burned on it, with his wife Nanna, who died of grief; Þórr hallowed the pyre with Mjöllnir
Poets call Baldr "Possessor of Hringhorni and Draupnir".

why.en: Baldr's funeral: the ship, the giantess, the pyre.
How poets name Baldr by his ship and ring.

hook.en: First of the valkyries Óðinn names to bring him the horn in Valhöll.

value.en: A valkyrie, named first in Óðinn's list of those who bring drink to the einherjar
Snorri: these valkyries serve in Valhöll, bear drink and look after the table and the ale-cups
Snorri: Óðinn sends the valkyries to every battle; they choose who is to die and decide the victory
Skalds build phrases on her name: battle is Hristar hreggöld, Hrist's storm-age, and a woman is mjaðar Hrist, the Hrist of mead ("the Mead's bright Valkyr" in the English).

why.en: Óðinn names the valkyries, Hrist first.
Snorri on the valkyries' work in Valhöll.

hook.en: The strongest giant, with a heart and head of stone, who raced Óðinn into Ásgarðr and then fought Þórr in a duel.

value.en: The strongest of the giants. His heart is hard stone with three points, his head and shield are stone, and his weapon is a whetstone.
The horse Gullfaxi, which he claims is better than Sleipnir.
He chases Óðinn into Ásgarðr, gets drunk, and boasts he will carry Valhöll to Jötunheimar, kill the gods, and take Freyja and Sif home.
In the duel at Grjótúnagarðar, Þjálfi tricks him into standing on his shield; Mjöllnir smashes his skull, but a piece of his whetstone lodges in Þórr's head.
His horse Gullfaxi, which Þórr gives to his young son Magni for lifting the dead giant's leg off him.
Þórr boasts of the fight in Hárbarðsljóð: the giant "whose head of stone was made".

why.en: A drunk giant in Valhöll, served by Freyja.
The duel: whetstone against hammer.
A three-night-old boy lifts the giant's leg.
The giantess grinders boast of Hrungnir and his father as hard men.

hook.en: A giant who comes from the east at Ragnarök with his shield raised; Snorri makes him the helmsman of Naglfar.

value.en: In Völuspá he drives from the east holding his shield before him, as the serpent writhes and Naglfar is loosed.
Snorri says he steers Naglfar, the ship made of dead men's nails. In Völuspá the ship from the east bringing Múspell's people is steered by Loki.
Snorri brings him to the field Vígríðr with all the frost giants behind him.

why.en: Hrymr's one appearance in Völuspá.
Snorri's Ragnarök: Naglfar afloat, Hrymr at the helm.

hook.en: The young runner who beat Þórr's swift servant three times — because he was Útgarða-Loki's own thought.

value.en: A young lad whom Útgarða-Loki calls to race against Þjálfi.
He wins three heats; by the last, Þjálfi has not reached halfway when Hugi turns at the end.
Útgarða-Loki reveals that Hugi was his own thought, and Þjálfi could not hope to match its speed.

why.en: The third race.
Who Hugi really was.

hook.en: One of Óðinn's two ravens, sent out each dawn over the world, though Óðinn fears he may not come back.

value.en: One of the two ravens who sit on Óðinn's shoulders and tell him all they see and hear; the other is Muninn
Óðinn sends them out at daybreak to fly over the whole world and they return by the morning meal; so he is called Raven-God (Hrafnaguð)
Óðinn's words: “I fear for Huginn lest he fare not back”, yet he fears more for Muninn
An old verse fragment: two ravens fly from Óðinn's shoulders, “Huginn to the hanged” and Muninn to the corpses
His name is also a poets' word for any raven

why.en: Snorri explains the ravens and Óðinn's name Raven-God.
Óðinn's worry for his two ravens, in his own verse.
The ravens fly off to the gallows and the battlefield.

hook.en: The spring in the middle of the cold world, source of the rivers, where the snake Níðhöggr torments the dead.

value.en: A spring in the middle of Niflheimr, made "many ages" before the earth; rivers flow from it, and one of them, Gjöll, runs nearest Hel's gates
Under the root of Yggdrasill that stands over Niflheimr
Níðhöggr, with more serpents than any tongue can tell
The hart Eikþyrnir stands on Valhöll; drops from his horns fall into Hvergelmir and become the rivers
After Ragnarök "it is worst in Hvergelmir", where the cursed snake tears dead men's bodies

why.en: The cold world and its well, before the earth existed.
Eikþyrnir's horns feed the rivers.

hook.en: A frost-bearded giant at the edge of heaven who took Þórr fishing — and cut the line on the World Serpent.

value.en: East of Élivágar, at the edge of heaven.
In Hymiskviða Týr calls him his father; Snorri makes Týr Óðinn's son. Hymir's mother has nine hundred heads.
He owns a kettle a league deep, which Þórr carries off so that Ægir can brew ale for the gods.
He takes Þórr fishing. Þórr baits his hook with an ox head and catches the World Serpent; in Snorri the terrified Hymir cuts the line.
His drinking cup will not break on stone, only on his own skull, which is harder.
In Snorri, Þórr punches him overboard. In Hymiskviða he comes after Þórr with a band of many-headed giants, and Þórr kills them all.

why.en: Hymir comes home, his beard frozen.
The fishing trip, and the cut line.
The cup that only Hymir's head can break.
Týr names the giant as his father.

hook.en: A cave-dwelling giantess whom Freyja wakes to recite a young man's ancestry — and who insults Freyja all the while.

value.en: A cave. Freyja wakes her and calls her "sister".
A wolf; Freyja asks her to let it run beside her own boar.
She recites the ancestry of Freyja's favourite Óttarr, and ends: "And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!"
She mocks Freyja: says the boar Freyja rides is her lover Óttarr, and that she runs about at night like the goat Heiðrún among bucks.
Freyja asks for memory-ale for Óttarr and threatens to ring her with fire. Hyndla answers that Freyja should bring him beer mixed with poison. Freyja says the curse will have no power.

why.en: Freyja wakes the giantess at dusk.
Hyndla sees through the boar.
Fire, and a poisoned gift.

hook.en: A giantess who rode a wolf with a viper for reins, and alone could launch Baldr's funeral ship.

value.en: A wolf, with a viper as reins. Four of Óðinn's berserks cannot hold the beast until they knock it down.
The gods send to Jötunheimar for her.
Baldr's ship Hringhorni will not move for the gods; she pushes it out at the first shove, so that fire flies from the rollers and all lands shake.
In Snorri's story Þórr wants to smash her head, but the gods ask peace for her. A skaldic verse, by contrast, lists Hyrrokkin among the giantesses Þórr has killed.

why.en: Baldr's funeral, and the giantess on the wolf.
A skald's list of Þórr's victims names her.

hook.en: The field at the heart of Ásgarðr where the gods first built — and where they meet again after Ragnarök.

value.en: In the middle of Ásgarðr (Snorri)
Völuspá: the gods met there, built altars and temples, set up forges and made tools
Snorri: the gods held council there and built their halls Glaðsheimr and Vingólf
After Ragnarök the surviving gods meet on Iðavöllr, talk of the old days, and find the gods' golden gaming pieces in the grass

why.en: The gods at work in the first days.
The gods meet again on Iðavöllr.

hook.en: She keeps the apples the gods eat to stay young. When a giant stole her, the gods turned grey and old.

value.en: Bragi
