In her ash-wood box she keeps the apples the gods bite when they grow old. Eating them makes them young again, and it will be so until Ragnarök. Poets call the apples the "Age-Elixir of the Æsir".
The giant Þjazi had Loki in his power and made him swear to get Iðunn out of Ásgarðr. Loki lured her into a wood with talk of better apples. Þjazi, in eagle shape, carried her off to Þrymheimr.

Without her the gods quickly grew grey and old. Loki borrowed Freyja's hawk-plumage, turned Iðunn into a nut and flew her home. Þjazi chased them, his feathers caught fire, and the gods killed him inside their gate.
"Keeper of the Apples" and "Spoil of the Giant Thjazi"
Snorri gives no parents. The late poem Hrafnagaldr Óðins makes her "of alfen race", the youngest of Ívaldi's elder children.

why.en: Loki lures her out with talk of better apples.
The rescue: Iðunn as a nut, a hawk, an eagle and a fire.
In Lokasenna, Loki says she embraced her brother's killer. She answers calmly.

hook.en: A dwarf known only through his sons, who built Freyr's folding ship and Óðinn's spear.

value.en: Father of the dwarves called "Ívaldi's sons"; he does nothing himself in the stories
His sons made Skíðblaðnir, best of ships, for Freyr "in days of old"
At Loki's request they also made Sif's hair of gold and the spear Gungnir
In the late poem Forspjallsljóð, Iðunn is "of alfen race", "the youngest of Ivaldi's elder children".

why.en: The oldest witness: Ívaldi's sons shape Skíðblaðnir.
Loki fetches gold hair, ship and spear from Ívaldi's sons.
A late poem links Iðunn to Ívaldi and the elves.

hook.en: A giantess and mother of Magni, Þórr's son who at three nights old lifted Hrungnir's leg off his father.

value.en: Magni, son of Þórr and Járnsaxa.
Óðinn says Þórr was wrong to give the horse Gullfaxi to "the son of a giantess" instead of to his father.
Poets call Sif "Co-Wife of Járnsaxa", and a wolf "the black steed of Járnsaxa".
Völuspá in skamma names a Járnsaxa among the nine giantess mothers of Heimdallr; it may be another figure.

why.en: Her baby son outdoes all the gods.
Sif named as her rival.

hook.en: Ironwood: a forest east of Miðgarðr where an old giantess breeds the wolves that hunt the sun and moon.

value.en: East of Miðgarðr
Troll-women called Járnviðjur, and an old giantess who bears many giant sons, all in wolf shape
The wolves that chase the sun and moon, Sköll and Hati, come from there; the mightiest of the brood, Mánagarmr, will swallow the moon

why.en: "The giantess old in Ironwood sat."
Snorri on the wolf-brood.

hook.en: Earth as a person: mother of Þórr, bride of Óðinn and daughter of Night.

value.en: Þórr; Þrymskviða calls him the son of Jörð
Daughter of Nótt (Night) and her second husband Ánarr; sister of Auðr and of Dagr (Day)
Óðinn: poets call the earth Óðinn's bride and co-wife of Frigg, Rindr and Gunnlöð
Counted among the Ásynjur, the goddesses
Poems call Þórr's mother Hlóðyn and Fjörgyn; Snorri lists both as names for the earth

why.en: Night's three marriages, and where Earth fits in.
All the ways a poet may name the earth.
The ferryman sends Þórr home past his mother Fjörgyn.

hook.en: Loki's serpent-child, thrown into the sea by Óðinn, which grew until it rings all the land and bites its own tail.

value.en: Child of Loki and the giantess Angrboða; sibling of Fenrir and Hel. Hymiskviða calls it the wolf's brother
The deep sea around all lands, where Óðinn threw it. It lies round the whole earth and bites its own tail
Þórr's great enemy. At Útgarða-Loki's hall it was disguised as the cat that Þórr could lift only one foot off the ground
Fishing with the giant Hymir, Þórr hooked it with an ox-head and hauled it to the gunwale; Hymir cut the line. Snorri doubts those who say Þórr then struck off its head
At Ragnarök it comes ashore in giant fury and blows venom over sky and sea. Þórr kills it, walks nine paces and falls dead from its venom
Miðgarðsormr, the Midgard Serpent; Skáldskaparmál lists Jörmungandr among the poetic names for serpents

why.en: Þórr and the serpent stare each other down across the boat.
The same fishing scene in verse: Þórr hammers the wolf's brother.
Útgarða-Loki reveals what the giant cat really was.
Þórr's last fight: he kills the serpent and dies of its venom.

hook.en: An old Gothic king who hanged his own son and had his son's bride trampled under horses.

value.en: "King Jörmunrekkr the Mighty"; in Hamðismál his riders are Goths
He sent his son Randvér to woo Svanhildr for him; believing Earl Bikki's report, he hanged Randvér and had Svanhildr trodden to death
Randvér sent him a hawk with its feathers plucked; seeing it, the king understood his kingdom was as helpless, "since he was old and childless"
Hamðir and Sörli cut off his hands and feet as he slept; he woke, called his men, and had the brothers stoned
Bragi the Old described the attack on him in a poem about a painted shield

why.en: He laughs, strokes his beard, and calls for his arms.
He boasts he would hang Hamðir and Sörli.
"Stone ye the men that steel will bite not."

hook.en: The giants' land, reached by going east, across the deep sea, or over icy rivers.

value.en: The home of giants. Þórr goes east over the deep sea to reach it; Gefjun fetches oxen "from the north" out of it; Þórr wades north over Élivágar from it
Giants, such as Nörfi, father of Night, and Þrymr, who hid Þórr's hammer
Völuspá: the gods' golden age lasted until three mighty giant-maidens came "out of Jötunheimar"; Snorri also blames women from Jötunheimr for spoiling it
Loki fetched Iðunn back from there; Freyr saw Gerðr there from Hliðskjálf
At Ragnarök "all Jötunheimr groans" while the gods hold council

why.en: Three giant-maidens end the golden age.
Þórr's journey east to the giants.

hook.en: A man shaped from the spittle of two peoples making peace, so wise that no question could defeat him.

value.en: When the Æsir and the Vanir made peace, both sides spat into one vat. The gods would not let this peace-token go to waste and shaped a man from it.
Wisdom: no one could ask him anything he could not answer. He travelled the world teaching people. Poetry is called "Kvasir's blood" after him.

The dwarves Fjalarr and Galarr killed him, ran his blood into two vats and the kettle Óðrerir, and mixed it with honey: whoever drinks that mead becomes a poet or a scholar. They told the Æsir he had choked on his own wisdom. Yet in Gylfaginning a Kvasir, "wisest of all", is alive when the Æsir hunt Loki, and works out the net from its ashes; Snorri does not explain.

why.en: Peace sealed in a vat of spittle, and a man made from it.
His murder, and how his blood became the mead of poetry.
Kvasir again, alive, reading the ashes of Loki's net.

hook.en: The gods' first iron fetter for the wolf Fenrir; he broke it the first time he kicked.

value.en: A very strong fetter the Æsir made when they saw how fast the wolf was growing
The wolf let them put it on him and broke it at his first kick
A proverb: "to loose out of Lædingr" is said when anything is exceeding hard.
Eddubrot also names Drómi and Læðingr as the two fetters that did not hold

why.en: Both failed fetters, and the proverbs they left.
A second brief account of the three fetters.

hook.en: Loki's mother, also called Nál; poems and Snorri often name him "Laufey's son".

value.en: Loki; his brothers are Býleistr and Helblindi
Loki's father is the giant Fárbauti
Nál
Her son's usual name: Loki "Laufey's son" in Lokasenna, "the son of Laufey" in Þrymskviða, Loki Laufeyjarson in Snorri

why.en: Snorri introduces Loki and his family.
"Loki, Laufey's son" speaks up in the bride-dressing scene.

hook.en: Snorri's light-elves: "fairer to look upon than the sun", living in Álfheimr in the sky.

value.en: Álfheimr, one of the places in heaven. In Grímnismál the gods gave Álfheimr to Freyr as a tooth-gift.
Being fairer than the sun; they are unlike the dark-elves in looks, and still more unlike in nature
Snorri believes that for now only light-elves live in the third heaven, Víðbláinn, where the hall Gimlé stands
The name occurs only in this chapter of Snorri. The poems speak of "elves" without light or dark, often paired with the gods: "How fare the gods, how fare the elves?"

why.en: Snorri's one description of light-elves and dark-elves.
Who lives in the highest heaven, for now.
Álfheimr given to Freyr as a child's tooth-gift.

hook.en: The man in Útgarða-Loki's hall who out-ate Loki, bones and trough included — because he was fire itself.

value.en: One of Útgarða-Loki's household, called from the bench to compete against Loki.
In the eating contest both reach the middle of the meat trough together, but Logi has eaten the bones and the trough as well.
Útgarða-Loki reveals that Logi was wildfire, which burns a trough as fast as meat.

why.en: The eating match.
Who Logi really was.

hook.en: A giant's son counted among the gods: he claims Óðinn as his blood-brother, brings about Baldr's death, and lies bound until Ragnarök.

value.en: Counted among the Æsir, though his father is a giant. Handsome, evil in spirit and endlessly cunning: he gets the gods into trouble, then out of it. Also called Loptr. In Lokasenna he reminds Óðinn that the two of them mixed their blood together long ago.
Son of the giant Fárbauti and of Laufey (or Nál); brother of Býleistr and Helblindi. His wife is Sigyn; their son is Nari or Narfi. Snorri also names a son Váli.

With the giantess Angrboða: the wolf Fenrir, the Miðgarðr serpent Jörmungandr, and Hel. Snorri says Loki had such dealings with the stallion Svaðilfari that he later gave birth to a grey, eight-legged foal: Óðinn's horse Sleipnir. The mare that lured the stallion away is not named, but is implied to be Loki.

Baldr's death. In a woman's shape he learns from Frigg that the mistletoe swore no oath, then tells blind Höðr where to shoot it. People think he was also the giantess Þökk, who would not weep Baldr out of Hel.

Hiding as a salmon, he is caught and bound over three stones with the guts of his son (Narfi's in Snorri, Váli's in the prose of Lokasenna). A snake drips venom on his face; Sigyn holds a bowl under it. At Ragnarök he fights Heimdallr and each kills the other.

why.en: Snorri's portrait: lovely to look at, evil in mind.
Loki reminds Óðinn of their oath of blood-brotherhood.
The mare's foal: how Sleipnir came to be.
Loki tells blind Höðr to honour Baldr and offers to aim his shot.
The binding, the venom, and Sigyn's bowl.

hook.en: Þórr's son by a giantess, who at three nights old lifted the dead Hrungnir's leg off his father.

value.en: Son of Þórr and the giantess Járnsaxa; brother of Móði. Þórr names himself "Magni's father".
At three nights old he heaves Hrungnir's leg off the trapped Þórr, and says he would have killed the giant with his fist
Þórr gives him Hrungnir's horse Gullfaxi as a reward. Óðinn says it was wrong to give it to "the son of a giantess" and not to his father.
He outlives Ragnarök: with Móði he will have Mjöllnir in the new world

why.en: The three-night-old boy who frees his father.
Óðinn complains about who got the horse.
Magni and Móði will hold Mjöllnir after the fall.
Þórr names himself: Óðinn's son, Magni's father.

hook.en: “Moon-Hound”, mightiest of the wolf-brood of Járnviðr, who will gorge on the dead and swallow the moon.

value.en: The mightiest of the wolves born to the old giantess in Járnviðr, east of Miðgarðr. Snorri has just said that Hati will take the moon; he does not say whether Hati and Mánagarmr are the same wolf.
He is filled with the flesh of all who die, swallows the moon and spatters heaven with blood; then the sun loses her shine and the winds roar
Snorri then quotes Völuspá, which does not name him: one of the brood is "The moon's taker in troll's likeness"

why.en: Snorri on the wolf-brood of Járnviðr and the Moon-Hound.
The Völuspá lines Snorri builds on.
Blood on the gods' seats, black sunshine, shifting weather.

hook.en: The Moon as a person: he steers the moon's course, and took two children from the earth to follow him.

value.en: Son of Mundilfari, brother of Sól (Sun)

He steers the course of the moon and rules its waxing and waning. He took up two children, Bil and Hjúki, as they walked from a well carrying a cask on a pole; they follow him, as can be seen from the earth.
The wolf Hati runs ahead of the sun, eager to seize the moon; Snorri also says a wolf, Mánagarmr, will swallow the moon and splash the sky with blood
In Alvíssmál the moon is called "Máni" by men and has other names among gods, giants, dwarves and elves

why.en: Mundilfari's children set in the sky; Bil and Hjúki.
In the beginning the moon did not know its own power.
The wolf-brood of Ironwood and the Moon-Hound.

hook.en: Brewed by dwarves from a murdered wise man's blood, it turns whoever drinks it into a poet or a scholar.

value.en: Kvasir's blood mixed with honey by the dwarves Fjalarr and Galarr, in Óðrerir, Són and Boðn. Whoever drinks it becomes a skald or a scholar.
The dwarves gave it to the giant Suttungr to save their lives. He hid it in Hnitbjörg, guarded by his daughter Gunnlöð.
Óðinn, calling himself Bölverkr, worked a summer for Suttungr's brother Baugi, crept into the mountain as a snake, lay three nights with Gunnlöð and drank all three vessels dry
He flew home as an eagle and spat the mead into the gods' vats. Some went out behind him: that is "the poetaster's part", free to anyone.
Óðinn gave it to the Æsir and to people who can compose; so poetry is "Odin's Booty and Find, and his Drink and Gift", and "Kvasir's Blood".
Hávamál tells it too: the speaker says Gunnlöð gave him the drink on a golden stool and he repaid her badly; the poem adds that Óðinn left her in grief.

why.en: How the mead was made, and what it does.
The eagle chase and the poetaster's share.
Óðinn remembers Gunnlöð and the golden stool.

hook.en: Fenja's companion at the mill Grótti, who sang as she ground — first peace for a king, then his doom.

value.en: A giant-born woman, called with Fenja "fore-knowing" and "The Mighty Maidens", held as slaves.
Bought with Fenja by King Fróði from King Fjölnir in Sweden, because they are big and strong.
In Gróttasöngr it is Menja who starts the grinding song, wishing Fróði wealth and a peace where no one harms another.
With Fenja she grinds an army against Fróði; the sea-king Mýsingr takes them and has them grind salt until his ship sinks.
In Sigurðarkviða gold is called "Menja's wealth".

why.en: Menja's grinding song of peace.
The song turns: fire and an army are coming.
The mill breaks in two.

hook.en: Not the whole earth but a fence: the gods built it from the giant Ymir's eyebrows to keep the giants out.

value.en: A stronghold round the inner earth, made from Ymir's eyebrows, against the hostility of the giants
The earth is round, with the deep sea around it; the giants got the land along the outer shore, Miðgarðr is inside
People: Askr and Embla's descendants received a dwelling-place "under Midgard"
Völuspá: the sons of Burr lifted up the land: "Mithgarth the mighty there they made"
Járnviðr lies east of it; the serpent in the sea is the Miðgarðsormr, and Þórr is called Miðgarðr's defender

why.en: The shape of the world: sea, giants' shore, inner fence.
The making of Miðgarðr in Völuspá.

hook.en: Keeper of the well of wisdom under the world tree; Óðinn gave one of his eyes for a single drink.

value.en: The owner of Mímir's well, where wisdom and understanding are kept, under the root of Yggdrasill that turns toward the frost-giants. He is full of lore because he drinks from the well out of the horn Gjallarhorn.
Óðinn asked for one drink from the well and had to leave his eye as a pledge; every morning Mímir drinks mead from "Valfather's wage" — the pledged eye
When Ragnarök begins, Óðinn rides to Mímir's well to take his counsel. Völuspá says Óðinn talks with Mímir's head.
Also Mímr: Völuspá speaks of Míms höfuð (Mímr's head) and Míms synir (Mímr's sons)
In Sigrdrífumál his head speaks "words of truth". Poets call Óðinn "Friend of Mímir".

why.en: The well under the world tree and the price of a drink.
The seeress tells Óðinn she knows where his eye is hidden.
Ragnarök: Óðinn's last counsel at Mímir's well.
Heimdallr's horn sounds while Óðinn talks with Mímir's head.
Mímir's head speaks its first wise word.

hook.en: The well of wisdom under the giants' root of the ash, where Óðinn left an eye as payment for one drink.

value.en: A well under the root of Yggdrasill that turns toward the frost-giants; wisdom and understanding are hidden in it
Mímir, who owns the well and drinks from it with the horn Gjallarhorn, and so is full of lore
Óðinn got a drink only by leaving his eye in pledge; Mímir drinks "Mead from the pledge of Othin each morn"
At Ragnarök Óðinn rides to Mímir's well to take counsel

why.en: The seeress: I know where Óðinn's eye is hidden.
Snorri's account of the well and the pledge.

hook.en: A valkyrie Óðinn names when he wants someone to bring him his drinking horn.

value.en: A valkyrie: "Hrist and Mist I would have bear the horn to me", says Óðinn in Grímnismál
Snorri: these valkyries serve in Valhöll, bear drink and look after the table and the ale-cups
Snorri: Óðinn sends the valkyries to every battle; they choose who is to die and decide the victory
Her name turns up in poets' phrases: swords are "Mist's leeks", and Helgakviða speaks of "Mist's horse"

why.en: Óðinn's list of serving valkyries, Mist second.
Snorri explains what these valkyries do in Valhöll.

hook.en: Þórr's hammer: it never misses, always returns to his hand, and its handle is a little too short.

value.en: Made by the dwarf Sindri, while Brokkr worked the bellows, to win a bet with Loki. The gods judged it the best of all the treasures and the greatest defence against the frost-giants.
Striking as hard as Þórr likes without breaking; when thrown it never misses and always comes back to his hand; it can be made small enough to keep in his shirt. Its flaw: the handle is rather short.
Þórr. It is one of his three treasures, with the belt of strength and the iron gloves he cannot do without when he grips the handle.
Killing giants (the wall-builder, Hrungnir), hallowing Þórr's goats back to life, and hallowing Baldr's funeral pyre
Stolen by the giant Þrymr and hidden eight miles under the earth; Þórr got it back dressed as a bride, and killed Þrymr with it
After Ragnarök Þórr's sons Móði and Magni will have it

why.en: What the hammer can do, and its one flaw.
Þórr gets his hammer back at the wedding feast.
Snorri's list of Þórr's three treasures.

hook.en: A son of Þórr who, with his brother Magni, will hold Mjöllnir after the old gods fall.

value.en: Son of Þórr, brother of Magni; his mother is not named
He survives Ragnarök and comes to Iðavöllr, where Ásgarðr was; he and Magni will have Mjöllnir
Little else is told. Hymiskviða calls Þórr the father of Móði as he breaks through the floor.

why.en: The giant's answer: who inherits the hammer.
The renewed world, where Þórr's sons bring Mjöllnir.
Þórr as father of Móði in the kettle story.

hook.en: Óðinn's second raven, who flies over the world with Huginn every day; it is Muninn whom Óðinn fears for most.

value.en: One of the two ravens who sit on Óðinn's shoulders and tell him the news; the other is Huginn
Both fly every day over the wide earth, sent out at daybreak and back by the morning meal
Óðinn fears Huginn may not come back, “Yet watch I more for Muninn”
An old verse fragment sends Huginn to the hanged and “Muninn to the corpses”
His name is also a poets' word for any raven; a skald's verse has "dark Muninn" drinking blood from wounds

why.en: Óðinn's fear for his ravens, in his own verse.
What the ravens do for Óðinn each day.
Muninn on the battlefield, in a skald's verse.

hook.en: The bright, burning world in the south, guarded by Surtr with a flaming sword.

value.en: The first world, in the south: light and hot, burning, and closed to anyone not born there
Múspell, and Múspellsheimr
Surtr, who sits at its border to guard it, holding a flaming sword
Its sparks lit the southern part of Ginnungagap; the gods set them in the sky to light heaven and earth
At Ragnarök Múspell's sons ride out and Bifröst breaks under them; in Völuspá Múspell's people come over the sea from the east, with Loki steering

why.en: Surtr at the border with his flaming sword.
Múspell's people sail to the last battle.

hook.en: The largest ship of all, built from dead men's uncut nails; it floats free when the world ends.

value.en: The largest ship; Múspell has it
Made of dead men's nails, so a man who dies with uncut nails adds to it; gods and men want it finished as late as possible
At Ragnarök the sea floods the land and Naglfar floats loose. Snorri says the giant Hrymr steers it.
Völuspá only says Hrymr comes from the east and "Naglfar is loose"; the next stanza has another ship with Múspell's people and Loki at the helm

why.en: The nail-ship and the warning to trim your nails.
The verse Snorri builds on.

hook.en: Baldr's wife's heart burst with grief when his body was carried to the ship. She burned on his pyre.

value.en: Daughter of Nepr, wife of Baldr and mother of Forseti
When Baldr's body was carried out onto the ship, she burst with grief and died. She was laid on his pyre and burned with him.
When Hermóðr visits the dead Baldr, she sends gifts back with him: a linen robe and more for Frigg, and a gold finger-ring for Fulla.
She is one of the goddesses at Ægir's feast. Poets call Frigg her mother-in-law.
Hyndluljóð names a Nanna, daughter of Nökkvi, among Óttarr's ancestors. Nothing there links her to Baldr.

why.en: Baldr's funeral: the ship, the giantess, and Nanna's death.
Gifts sent back from Hel: Baldr's ring and Nanna's presents.

hook.en: A giant of Jötunheimar and the father of Night, who was black and dark like her kin.

value.en: A giant (jötunn) who lived in Jötunheimar. Not the same as Loki's son Narfi or Nari.
Nótt (Night), who was black and dark, as befitted her kin
Nörfi; in Vafþrúðnismál, "the night was begotten by Nor"

why.en: Night's family, starting with her giant father.
The giant Vafþrúðnir names the fathers of Day and Night.

hook.en: Loki and Sigyn's son, Nari or Narfi, whose guts in Snorri's telling became the bonds of his father.

value.en: Two beings bear the name Narfi: this son of Loki, and Nörfi or Narfi, a giant of Jötunheimar who fathered Nótt (Night)
Son of Loki and his wife Sigyn; brother of Váli
Narfi or Nari: Gylfaginning gives both, and Skáldskaparmál lists Nari among Loki's children
Snorri: his brother Váli, turned into a wolf, tears him apart, and the gods bind Loki with his guts, which turn to iron
In the closing prose of Lokasenna it is Narfi who is turned into a wolf, and Loki is bound with Váli's guts

why.en: Loki's portrait, ending with his wife Sigyn and their son.
The binding of Loki in Snorri's version.
The binding in Lokasenna's version, with the roles reversed.
The other Narfi: a giant, the father of Night.

hook.en: The serpent gnawing the world-ash's root from below, exchanging envious words with the eagle above and tearing at the dead.

value.en: Under the root of Yggdrasill that stands over Niflheimr, in the spring Hvergelmir, with more snakes than any tongue can count
He gnaws the ash from below, while a hart bites it above and its side rots
The squirrel Ratatoskr carries the eagle's words down to him; Snorri calls them envious words
In Völuspá he sucks the corpses of the dead at the hall on Náströnd, where oath-breakers and murderers wade; Snorri puts this in Hvergelmir
Völuspá ends with the dark dragon flying up from Niðafjöll, bearing corpses in his feathers
Skáldskaparmál's list of names for serpents

why.en: The ash suffers more than men know: bitten above, gnawed below.
Eagle, hawk, squirrel, harts and snakes: the tree's creatures.
The seeress sees him feeding on the dead.
The last image of Völuspá: the dragon in flight.

hook.en: The world of mist and cold, made before the earth: source of ice and rivers, and for Snorri, of the dead.

value.en: Made "many ages" before the earth was shaped; the spring Hvergelmir lies in the middle of it
Cold and "all terrible things" came from it; its rime met the heat from Múspell in Ginnungagap, and Ymir came alive
Under one root of Yggdrasill
Hel: Óðinn cast her into Niflheimr and gave her power over nine worlds, to receive those who die of sickness or old age
Snorri: wicked men go to Hel and from there to Niflhel, "down in the ninth world". The giant Vafþrúðnir says he has been to nine worlds, down to Niflhel

why.en: Cold from the north, heat from the south: life begins.
Hel's hall and her servants, named one by one.

hook.en: A Vanir god handed to the Æsir as a hostage, who calms wind and sea and could not bear the mountain wolves.

value.en: He rules the course of the wind and calms sea and fire. People call on him for sea voyages, for hunting and fishing, and for wealth.
Not one of the Æsir by birth. He grew up among the Vanir, who gave him to the gods as a hostage; they took Hœnir in exchange.
Nóatún, his hall in the sky
The giantess Skaði. She chose him by his feet alone, hoping for Baldr. She could not sleep by the sea for the gulls, he hated her mountains, and she went back to them.
Freyr and Freyja. Loki claims Njörðr had his son by his own sister.
When the world ends he will go back home to the wise Vanir

why.en: Nine nights in the mountains: wolves howling instead of swans singing.
Skaði picks a husband by looking only at feet.
Loki mocks him as a hostage; Njörðr's proud reply follows in the next stanza.
A giant explains where Njörðr came from and where he will go.

hook.en: Njörðr's home by the sea, where his mountain-bred wife Skaði could not sleep for the cries of the gulls.

value.en: Njörðr's dwelling, in heaven
Njörðr and Skaði agreed to spend nine nights in Þrymheimr and nine in Nóatún. He hated the wolves' howling in the mountains; she could not sleep by the sea for the seabirds
Njörðr's children Freyr and Freyja were born there
In Grímnismál, the eleventh dwelling; Þrymr calls Freyja "The daughter of Njorth out of Noatun"

why.en: Skaði's verse: the gull wakes me every morning.
Njörðr's high-timbered shrine.

hook.en: One of four dwarves set under the corners of the sky, which was made from a giant's skull. His name means "North".

value.en: One of four dwarves the gods set under the four corners of the sky: Austri, Vestri, Norðri, Suðri (East, West, North, South)
Under a corner of the sky, which the gods made from the skull of the giant Ymir
Poets may call the sky the "helm" of Vestri, Austri, Suðri and Norðri, or the "task" or "burden" of the dwarves
The name also stands in Völuspá's list of dwarves

why.en: The gods build the sky from Ymir's skull.
How poets name the sky after the four dwarves.

hook.en: Night, a dark giant's daughter, rides round the earth; each morning her horse's foam falls as dew.

value.en: The giant Nörfi or Narfi, who lived in the land of giants; she is dark, like her kin
Three in turn: Naglfari, father of Auðr; Ánarr, father of Jörð (Earth); and Dellingr of the Æsir's kin, father of Dagr (Day)
Óðinn gave her and her son Day each a horse and a chariot and set them in the sky to ride round the earth
Hrímfaxi, who drops foam from his bit every morning; from it comes the dew
Alvíssmál gives night's names among gods, giants, elves and dwarves

why.en: Night's family, and her nightly ride.
Hrímfaxi and the dew in the dales.
What every race calls the night.

hook.en: Atli's sister, who loved Gunnarr in secret and heard his harp across the sound too late to save him.

value.en: Sister of Atli
Gunnarr sought her as his wife and offered rich gifts, but Atli would take no bride-price from Gjúki's son
Gunnarr, her lover: Atli's men found them together in the dark wood. When she heard his harp from Hlésey she sailed to help, but Atli's mother had already dug into his heart
She sang strong charms over Borgný, who could not give birth, and then told her own story

why.en: The death of Gunnarr as Oddrún saw it.
Brynhildr foretells their secret love.
Her closing line: "Oddrun's lament is ended now."

hook.en: The one-eyed chief of the gods, who pledged an eye for one drink of wisdom and hung nine nights on a tree.

value.en: Son of Borr and the giantess Bestla, daughter of the giant Bölþorn; his brothers are Vili and Vé. Frigg is his wife.
One eye. He asked for one drink from Mímir's well and had to leave his eye there as a pledge.
The spear Gungnir, made by dwarfs, the sons of Ívaldi; it never stops in its thrust.
Sleipnir, the eight-legged horse, best of the gods' horses.
Valhöll, which he gives to those who fall in battle as his adopted sons; but Freyja takes half of the slain, and Óðinn half. From his high seat Hliðskjálf he sees over all the worlds.

In Hávamál he hangs nine nights on a windy tree, wounded by a spear, "myself to myself", and takes up the runes. In Snorri he wins the mead of poetry from the giant Suttungr after three nights with Suttungr's daughter Gunnlöð, and gives it to the gods and to poets. Two ravens, Huginn and Muninn, sit on his shoulders and bring him news from all the world.
At Ragnarök he rides first, with gold helmet and Gungnir, against the wolf Fenrir. The wolf swallows him; his son Víðarr avenges him.

why.en: Why Óðinn has one eye: the pledge at Mímir's well.
Óðinn speaks of hanging nine nights on the tree.
How Óðinn, as Bölverkr, wins the mead and flies off as an eagle.
His two ravens fly over the world each day and report.
Ragnarök: Óðinn rides out against the wolf and is swallowed.

hook.en: Freyja's husband, who went away on long journeys; her tears for him are red gold.

value.en: Freyja
A daughter, Hnoss
Going away. Freyja weeps red gold for him and searched for him among strange peoples, taking many names
Known almost only through Freyja: a skald calls her "Ódr's Bed-Mate", Völuspá calls her "Oth's bride" (Óðs mey), and Hyndla taunts her that she ran after Óðr, always longing

why.en: Everything Snorri says of Óðr, in a few lines about Freyja.
The gods ask who gave Óðr's maiden, Freyja, to the giants.
A skald calls Freyja wife of Óðr and mother of Hnoss.

hook.en: The kettle that caught the murdered Kvasir's blood; in Hávamál the name seems to mean the mead itself.

value.en: In Snorri, the kettle into which the dwarves Fjalarr and Galarr let Kvasir's blood run; the two vats were Són and Boðn
Óðinn, lying three nights with Gunnlöð, emptied Óðrerir in his first draught
Poetry can be called "liquid of Ódrerir", or the "Sea, or Liquid of the Dwarves", because Kvasir's blood lay in Óðrerir before it became mead.
In Hávamál the speaker, Óðinn, says "Othrörir now has up been brought" to the world of men, and that he got a drink of the mead "Poured out from Othrörir".

why.en: The dwarves fill the kettle.
Óðinn drains it in one draught.
Óðinn's own words: Óðrerir brought up to men.

hook.en: A shape-changer who fished in otter form, until Loki's stone killed him and the gods had to pay in gold.

value.en: Son of Hreiðmarr; brother of Fáfnir and Reginn
He often went into Andvari's waterfall in the shape of an otter; he was eating a salmon with his eyes shut when the gods passed
Loki killed him with a stone and boasted of getting an otter and a salmon with one throw; the gods skinned him
His skin had to be filled and covered with gold, so poets call gold "otter's ransom" (otrgjöld)

why.en: Snorri's telling: the otter, the salmon and Loki's stone.
Reginn tells it as the death of "a brother of ours".

hook.en: Ægir's wife, who owns a net that catches everyone who goes to sea; she and Ægir have nine daughters.

value.en: Wife of Ægir. They have nine daughters, among them Himinglæva, Dúfa, Blóðughadda and Kólga; poets use their names in phrases for the sea.
Danger at sea: in Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar a troll-woman would have given a king's men to Rán, and in Helgakviða Hundingsbana I a ship is wrenched from Rán's grip
A net with which she catches everyone who goes to sea. Loki borrows it to catch the dwarf Andvari, who lives in a waterfall in the shape of a pike.
Known mostly from poets' phrases: the sea is "husband of Rán" and "Rán's road", and gold is the light of Ægir and Rán

why.en: Loki borrows Rán's net to catch Andvari.
The names of the nine daughters of Ægir and Rán.
A troll-woman nearly gives a king's crew to Rán.

hook.en: A squirrel running up and down the world-ash, carrying the eagle's words down to the serpent below.

value.en: A squirrel (íkorni) on the ash Yggdrasill
He carries the words of the eagle at the top of the tree down to Níðhöggr at the bottom
Snorri calls these “envious words” (öfundarorð), passed between the eagle and Níðhöggr

why.en: Óðinn names the squirrel and his errand.
Snorri's tour of the creatures living in the ash.

hook.en: A dwarf-sized smith who fostered Sigurðr and forged his sword, then urged him to kill Fáfnir for the gold.

value.en: Son of Hreiðmarr; brother of Fáfnir and Otr; his sisters were Lyngheiðr and Lofnheiðr
Smith to King Hjálprekr; "more ingenious than all other men, and a dwarf in stature", wise, fierce and skilled in magic
Forging the sword Gramr for Sigurðr and urging him to kill Fáfnir
His share of the gold: Fáfnir took it all and told him to leave or die like their father
The sword Refill, in Snorri; in Fáfnismál he cuts out Fáfnir's heart with a sword called Riðill
After drinking Fáfnir's blood he lay down to sleep; the birds warned Sigurðr that he planned betrayal, and Sigurðr cut off his head

why.en: Reginn tells the boy Sigurðr the story of the otter's ransom.
A bird sings that Reginn means to betray the youth.
Sigurðr tells him: you hid in the heather while I fought.

hook.en: A valkyrie known only from one list: the last of those who bring ale to the dead warriors in Valhöll.

value.en: A valkyrie, last in the Grímnismál list that Snorri also quotes
Bringing ale to the einherjar, the fallen warriors in Valhöll
Snorri: Óðinn sends the valkyries to every battle; they choose who is to die and decide the victory

why.en: Her only appearance in the poems.
What Snorri says all valkyries do.

hook.en: A wandering god sleeps between three couples; nine months later the thrall, the farmer and the earl are born.

value.en: Rígr is the name taken by Heimdallr, says the prose before Rígsþula: an old, wise and strong god walking along the seashore
At three houses he sits and sleeps between husband and wife for three nights; nine months later a son is born: Þræll to Ái and Edda, Karl to Afi and Amma, Jarl to Faðir and Móðir
From Þræll come the thralls, from Karl the free farmers. Jarl he claims as his own son, teaches him runes and gives him his name.
His grandson Konr, Jarl's youngest son, wins the right to be called Rígr too

why.en: The prose that names the wandering god Heimdallr.
The first son: dark Þræll, ancestor of the thralls.
Rígr comes out of the thicket to claim Jarl.
Völuspá calls all people, high and low, "Heimdall's sons".

hook.en: Mother of Váli, the son of Óðinn who at one night old fights to avenge Baldr.

value.en: Váli, by Óðinn
In Baldrs draumar the seeress foretells that Rindr will bear Váli in Vestrsalir, and that at one night old he will bring Baldr's slayer to the pyre
Óðinn. Poets name her with Jörð and Gunnlöð as his partners besides Frigg. One skald says "Odin wrought charms on Rindr": a story the Eddas do not tell.
Counted among the Ásynjur, the goddesses

why.en: The seeress's unwilling prophecy of Rindr's son.
Kormákr's half-line about Óðinn's magic on Rindr.

hook.en: A farmer's daughter given to Þórr with her brother Þjálfi, as payment for a lamed goat.

value.en: Daughter of a farmer; sister of Þjálfi.
After her brother cracks a goat's bone, the farmer gives both children to Þórr; they become his servants and follow him always.
She goes with Þórr, Loki and Þjálfi into the great forest on the way to Útgarðr.
Poets call Þórr "Master of Thjálfi and Röskva".

why.en: The night at the farm.
The journey east begins.

hook.en: The boar of Valhöll: boiled every day to feed the dead warriors, and whole again by evening.

value.en: A boar whose flesh feeds the einherjar in Valhöll; however many they are, it never runs short
He is boiled every day and is whole again at evening
The cook is Andhrímnir and the kettle Eldhrímnir; few know what food the warriors live on
In the late poem Forspjallsljóð the gods themselves are sated with Sæhrímnir at a feast

why.en: Snorri on feeding the endless host of Valhöll.
The verse naming cook, kettle and boar.

hook.en: The second of the goddesses. Every day she drinks with Óðinn from golden cups where cool waves sound.

value.en: The second of the Ásynjur in Snorri's list of goddesses
Sökkvabekkr, "a great abode". Grímnismál names it as the fourth hall, with cool waves sounding over it.
She and Óðinn drink there together every day, glad, from golden cups

why.en: Óðinn and Sága drinking at Sökkvabekkr: all the poems say of her.
Snorri's single line on her.

hook.en: Þórr's wife had her hair cut off by Loki. The gold hair that replaced it grew like real hair.

value.en: Þórr. Poems often call him simply "Sif's mate".
Ullr, Þórr's stepson, and Þrúðr
Loki cut off all her hair out of malice. Þórr forced him to get new hair made of gold, and the sons of Ívaldi made it. It took root as soon as it touched her head. So poets call gold "Hair of Sif".
Poets call her "Fair-Haired Goddess". In his Prologue, Snorri says she was a prophetess named Síbíl.

In Lokasenna she offers Loki mead and asks him to leave her blameless. He claims he was her lover. In Hárbarðsljóð, Hárbarðr also taunts Þórr that Sif has a lover at home. Both claims are insults made in a quarrel.
The drunken giant Hrungnir boasted that he would kill the gods and take only Freyja and Sif home with him

why.en: Why gold is "Sif's hair": Loki's prank and Þórr's threat.
The new hair is judged among the gods' treasures.
Sif's peace offering to Loki, and the sting in his reply.

hook.en: Völsungr's son, so hardy he could drink poison unharmed; father of Sinfjötli, Helgi and Sigurðr.

value.en: Son of Völsungr. With Borghildr he had Helgi; with Hjördís, Sigurðr. Sinfjötli was his eldest son and Hámundr a third
Poison could not harm him outside or in; his sons could resist it only on the skin
King in Frankland; he lived long in Borghildr's realm in Denmark before going back south
A sword that Óðinn gave him, says Hyndluljóð
He fell in battle against the sons of Hundingr; Sigurðr later avenged him by killing Lyngvi Hundingsson

why.en: "Let it trickle through your beard, Son!" Then Sinfjötli dies.
Sigmundr's gilded ships, woven into a tapestry.

hook.en: A valkyrie who refused the husband her father chose — and later lay a night in her dead husband's burial mound.

value.en: Daughter of King Högni; sister of Dagr and Bragi. The prose says she was Sváfa born again
A valkyrie who "rode air and water"; she sheltered Helgi's ships in a storm off Gnipalundr
Promised by her father to Höðbroddr, whom she calls no more kingly than "the son of a cat", she rode to Helgi and chose him
Her father and her brother Bragi fell to Helgi; later her brother Dagr killed Helgi, and she cursed Dagr by the oaths he had broken
She made a bed in Helgi's mound and slept in the dead man's arms; she died young of grief, and was said to be reborn as the valkyrie Kára

why.en: Her curse on her brother Dagr.
Inside the mound: the dead king's ice-cold hands.
Her maid warns: the dead are stronger at night.

hook.en: He killed a dragon from a pit, tasted its heart and understood the birds — then died by his sworn brothers' plot.

value.en: Son of Sigmundr Völsungsson and Hjördís, daughter of Eylimi; fostered by the smith Reginn at King Hjálprekr's court
Grani, chosen from King Hjálprekr's herd; Grani would let no man but Sigurðr ride him
The sword Gramr, made by Reginn, so sharp it split Reginn's anvil
Killing Fáfnir on Gnitaheiðr; when the heart's blood touched his tongue he understood the birds, who warned him against Reginn, so he killed Reginn too
Guðrún, Gjúki's daughter; their children Sigmundr and Svanhildr. Snorri adds a daughter, Áslaug, raised by Heimir

Killed by Gotthormr, egged on by Brynhildr and his brothers. Snorri and Sigurðarkviða in skamma: stabbed asleep in bed beside Guðrún. The Brot: slain "south of the Rhine". Guðrúnarkviða II: Grani came back from the assembly without him. The prose 'Frá dauða Sigurðar' lists these versions

why.en: The dragon-killing from the trench, told plainly.
The dying Fáfnir asks who his killer is.
He finds a sleeping woman in armour inside a ring of light.
Mortally wounded, he hurls Gramr and cuts down his killer, Gotthormr.
The old editor admits the poems disagree on how he died.

hook.en: Loki's wife stands over her bound husband, holding a bowl to catch the snake's venom.

value.en: Loki. Poets call him "Husband of Sigyn".

Nari or Narfi. In Gylfaginning the gods turn his brother Váli into a wolf, Váli tears him apart, and his guts are used to bind Loki. The prose of Lokasenna reverses this: Loki is bound with Váli's guts, and Narfi becomes a wolf.
She holds a basin under the dripping venom while Loki lies bound. When she goes to empty it, the venom falls on his face, and his writhing shakes the earth. That is what people call earthquakes.
Völuspá's seeress sees her sitting by her bound husband, "nor is glad"
She is one of the goddesses at Ægir's feast

why.en: Loki's punishment and Sigyn's bowl, in Snorri's words.
The seeress's glimpse of Sigyn beside the bound Loki.
The same scene in the prose ending of Lokasenna.

hook.en: The dwarf smith who forged Þórr's hammer, Óðinn's dripping ring and Freyr's golden boar.

value.en: A dwarf smith, brother of Brokkr. Loki bet his head that Sindri could not make three treasures as good as those of Ívaldi's sons.
From a pigskin he made a boar with golden bristles, from gold the ring Draupnir, and from iron a hammer
Warning that the hammer would be spoiled if the bellows stopped; when they faltered, he said it had come close to ruining everything
The same name belongs to a hall of red gold on Niðafjöll where good people will live after Ragnarök; Völuspá speaks of a golden hall "for Sindri's race".

why.en: The whole forging, step by step, with the fly at work.
A golden hall of "Sindri's race" in the north.
Snorri's hall Sindri, a home for the good after the end.

hook.en: Sigmundr's eldest son, a master of insults, who died from the third horn of poison his stepmother handed him.

value.en: Eldest son of Sigmundr; brother of Helgi; stepson of Borghildr
Before Helgi's battle with Granmarr's sons he trades insults with Guðmundr across the water; Guðmundr calls him Siggeirr's stepson, who ate wolves' food and killed his own brothers
Poison could not harm him on the skin

He killed Borghildr's brother in a quarrel over a woman. At the funeral feast she brought him poison three times; Sigmundr told him to drink the third, and he died. Sigmundr carried the body to a fjord, where a man in a small boat took it aboard and vanished

why.en: 'Frá dauða Sinfjötla': the three horns and the strange ferryman.
His answer to Guðmundr: a flyting on the eve of battle.

hook.en: A giant's daughter came to Ásgarðr armed for revenge. She left with a husband she chose by looking only at his feet.

value.en: A giantess, daughter of the giant Þjazi, who married into the gods. She is counted among the goddesses, and a verse calls her "pure bride of the gods".

Njörðr. To settle her claim for her father's death, the gods let her choose a husband by his feet alone. She hoped to get Baldr. In Skírnismál she calls Njörðr's son Freyr their son (Old Norse okkarn mög, 'our son').

Þrymheimr, her father's home in the mountains. She and Njörðr agreed to spend nine nights there and nine nights at his home by the sea, but neither could bear the other's home, so she went back to the mountains.
She travels on skis with a bow and hunts animals. She is called the ski-goddess.
Her settlement also required the gods to make her laugh. Loki did it with a goat and a cord. Óðinn threw Þjazi's eyes into the sky as two stars.
When the gods bound Loki, she hung a venomous snake over his face. In Lokasenna she threatens him, and he claims she once invited him to her bed.

why.en: Skaði arrives in helmet and mail to avenge her father.
Choosing by the feet: she expects Baldr and gets Njörðr.
Her verse: sea-birds' screeching kept her from sleeping by the sea.
Skaði to Loki: cold counsel will always come from her home.

hook.en: Freyr's ship: it carries all the gods with their weapons, yet folds up like a cloth to fit in a pouch.

value.en: Made by the dwarves called Ívaldi's sons, who gave it to Freyr
A fair wind as soon as the sail is raised, wherever it is going; when not at sea it folds up like a cloth and goes in a pouch
The best of ships and the most skilfully made; Naglfar is the largest

why.en: Snorri's full description of the folding ship.
The verse Snorri draws on: the ship made for Freyr.
Loki gives the ship to Freyr before the gods.

hook.en: “Sheen-Mane”, the horse of Day, whose shining mane lights up all the sky and the earth.

value.en: The horse of Dagr (Day), son of Nótt
All the air and the earth are lit from his mane
Óðinn tells the giant Vafþrúðnir that Skinfaxi draws the day for men and is held the best of horses
Glaðr, in Skáldskaparmál; Glaðr is also the name of one of the gods' horses

why.en: Night, Day and their two horses.
Óðinn's answer about the horse of day.

hook.en: Freyr's servant, who rode through flickering fire into giant-land and won a bride for his master by threats.

value.en: Freyr's servant and his friend since youth. He tells Gerðr he is neither elf, nor god, nor one of the Vanir.
Freyr's horse, which carries him through the dark and the flickering flame around Gymir's house
Freyr's sword, which fights by itself: his price for the errand
Two errands: wooing Gerðr for Freyr, first with gifts and then with the sword and a curse of runes; and fetching the fetter Gleipnir from the dwarves when Óðinn needs it to bind Fenrir

why.en: Skírnir names his price: the horse and the sword.
He talks to his horse before riding into the dark.
The threats begin: the taming wand and exile from men.
The rune-curse he can carve, and uncarve.

hook.en: A valkyrie Óðinn sends, with Göndul, to choose which king of Yngvi's line will come to Valhöll.

value.en: A valkyrie in Völuspá's list of those ready to ride, and in Grímnismál among those who bring ale to the einherjar
In Eyvindr's poem, "Göndull and Skögull / Gauta-Týr sent / To choose from kings" who should go to Valhöll; Gauta-Týr is Óðinn.
Poets call battle "the Din of Skögul".
In the late poem Forspjallsljóð she pours out mead from Mímir's horns at the gods' feast

why.en: Óðinn sends two valkyries to fetch a king.
The seeress sees the valkyries ready to ride.
Óðinn names the valkyries who serve in Valhöll.

hook.en: The wolf who runs behind the sun, which is why, Snorri says, she hurries across the sky as if afraid.

value.en: A wolf who chases the sun. She fears him, and he will take her
In Grímnismál Sköll “follows the glittering god”, the sun, while Hati is the other wolf
Snorri says these wolves descend from an old giantess in Járnviðr who bears giant sons in wolf shape
At Ragnarök “the Wolf shall swallow the sun”; Snorri does not name the wolf there
Skalli, in a riddle-answer of Heiðreksgátur, where Skalli and Hatti run one before and one after the sun

why.en: Why the sun hurries: two wolves, one behind and one ahead.
The two sun-wolves in Óðinn's own verse.
Where the wolves come from: the old giantess of Járnviðr.

hook.en: A giant so huge that Þórr's party slept in his glove's thumb, and Þórr's hammer blows felt like falling leaves.

value.en: The name given by a huge giant met in the forest; Útgarða-Loki later says it was he who met them there.
The "hall" Þórr's party slept in was his glove, and the side room its thumb.
He ties the shared food bag so tightly that Þórr cannot undo a single knot — it was bound with iron wire.
Three hammer blows only make him ask whether a leaf, an acorn or twigs from birds fell on him. The blows struck a hill instead, leaving three square valleys.
He warns the party not to boast in Útgarðr, or better, to turn back.

why.en: The giant picks up his glove.
"Do birds sit in the tree above me?"
Þórr mocked for hiding in a glove; the giant is called Fjalarr.

hook.en: The youngest norn, who also rides out with the valkyries to choose who dies in battle.

value.en: The third of the three norns, with Urðr and Verðandi
With the other norns, in the hall by the well under Yggdrasill
Snorri calls her the youngest norn, who rides with Guðr and Róta to choose the slain and decide fights
A shield: in Völuspá's list of valkyries ready to ride, "Skuld bore the shield"

why.en: Skuld among the three norns at the world-tree.
Skuld again, named first among the valkyries ready to ride.
Snorri joins the two roles: youngest norn and chooser of the slain.

hook.en: Óðinn's grey eight-legged horse, best of all steeds, foaled by Loki after he lured away a giant's stallion as a mare.

value.en: Óðinn's horse: grey, with eight legs. “Of all steeds Sleipnir” is the best
Born to Loki, who in the shape of a mare lured the builder's stallion Svaðilfari away; Völuspá in skamma says the same
Óðinn rides him down to Niflhel to raise a dead seeress about Baldr's dreams
Hermóðr borrows him to ride to Hel for Baldr, and he leaps clear over Hel's gate
Óðinn's ride on him into Jötunheimar starts a race with the giant Hrungnir and his horse Gullfaxi
Sigrdrífumál says runes were cut on Sleipnir's teeth

why.en: How Sleipnir was born, quoted with Völuspá.
The mare in the wood and the runaway stallion.
Óðinn saddles Sleipnir for the ride down to Niflhel.
Hermóðr spurs Sleipnir over the gate of Hel.
Óðinn races Hrungnir all the way into Ásgarðr.

hook.en: A hall where cool waves sound overhead and Óðinn and Sága drink together every day from golden cups.

value.en: The fourth dwelling in Grímnismál; cool waters roar over it
Sága, a goddess; Snorri calls it "a great abode"
Óðinn and Sága drink there gladly every day from golden cups

why.en: Almost everything known about it, in one stanza.
Snorri lists Sága second among the goddesses.

hook.en: A girl named Sun by her proud father; the angry gods set her in the sky to drive the sun's horses.

value.en: Daughter of Mundilfari, sister of Máni (Moon); married to Glenr
She drives the horses Árvakr and Alsviðr, which draw the sun's chariot; the gods set cooling bellows under their shoulders
The wolf Sköll runs after her, and she flees in fear; he will catch her. At Ragnarök the wolf swallows the sun.
Before she is swallowed she bears a daughter as fair as she is, who will ride her mother's paths in the new world
Counted among the Ásynjur, the goddesses

why.en: How a man's pride put his children in the sky.
Why the sun hurries: something is chasing her.
At the beginning, the sun did not know where her halls were.
The sun's daughter, who will shine after the end.

hook.en: The third vessel of the mead of poetry, emptied with Óðinn's last draught.

value.en: One of two vats (with Boðn) that, with the kettle Óðrerir, took Kvasir's blood
With the third draught Óðinn emptied Són, and had all the mead
Poetry is called the liquid "of Són"; a skald says "of Són the Seedling" grows on his tongue.

why.en: Three nights, three draughts, three vessels.
"Of Són the Seedling": poetry growing in the poet's mouth.

hook.en: The wiser of two brothers: he slipped, caught himself with his hand, and understood too late what Erpr had meant.

value.en: Son of Guðrún and King Jónakr; brother of Hamðir and Erpr
"Wise was he ever": he would not quarrel with his mother, and foresaw that they rode to their deaths
After the brothers killed Erpr, Sörli stumbled and steadied himself with his hand: "Now the hand assists the foot"
With Hamðir he cut off Jörmunrekkr's hands and feet; the king had them stoned, and Sörli fell by the gable of the hall

why.en: Sörli refuses to trade words with his mother.
The stumble that explains Erpr's riddle.
The brothers' death, in two lines.

hook.en: One of four dwarves under the sky's corners; his name means simply "South".

value.en: One of four dwarves the gods set under the four corners of the sky: Austri, Vestri, Norðri, Suðri (East, West, North, South)
Under a corner of the sky, which the gods made from the skull of the giant Ymir
Poets may call the sky the "helm" of Vestri, Austri, Suðri and Norðri, or the "task" or "burden" of the dwarves
The name also stands in Völuspá's list of dwarves

why.en: The gods build the sky from Ymir's skull.
How poets name the sky after the four dwarves.

hook.en: The fire giant who guards the border of Múspell with a flaming sword, and will burn the world at Ragnarök.

value.en: He sits at the land's end of Múspell to guard it, holding a flaming sword.
Snorri says that at the end of the world he will overcome all the gods and burn the whole world with fire.
At Ragnarök he comes from the south with fire; his sword shines brighter than the sun. He rides first of the sons of Múspell, and Bifröst breaks under them.
Freyr fights him and falls, lacking the sword he gave away. The battlefield is Vígríðr, a hundred leagues each way.
His fire does not end everything: gods' sons live on "when Surtr's fire has sunk".

why.en: The guard at the edge of the fire world.
The seeress sees Surtr come from the south.
Freyr against Surtr, without his sword.
What remains after the fire.

hook.en: The giant who took the mead of poetry from two murderous dwarves, hid it in a mountain, and lost it to Óðinn.

value.en: Son of the giant Gillingr; brother of Baugi; father of Gunnlöð.
After the dwarves Fjalarr and Galarr kill his father, he leaves them on a skerry that the tide will cover. They buy their lives with the mead.
He keeps the mead at Hnitbjörg, with his daughter Gunnlöð as its guard.
He refuses his brother's hired man "Bölverkr" a single drop.
He chases Óðinn in eagle shape and almost catches him at Ásgarðr, but the mead is saved. Hávamál says Óðinn left Suttungr cheated of his drink.
Poets call poetry "Suttungr's mead" (Suttunga mjöðr) after him.

why.en: How the mead came to a giant.
The eagle chase to Ásgarðr.
Óðinn remembers talking his way through Suttungr's halls.
Frost giants come asking whether Suttungr killed Bölverkr.

hook.en: The giant builder's stallion, who hauled stone by night until a mysterious mare lured him into the woods.

value.en: The stallion of the builder who offered to wall the gods' stronghold in one winter; Loki advised letting him help
He hauled the stones by night and did twice the work of his master, so the wall was nearly done three days before summer
One evening a mare ran out of a wood and whinnied to him; he broke his traces and ran after her all night, and the work stopped
Sleipnir, whom Loki bore some time later

why.en: The builder's bargain: Freyja, the sun and the moon.
The mare appears, and the work comes to a halt.
The whole affair in two lines of verse.

hook.en: A valkyrie who named a silent prince, guarded him in battle, and would not take another man after him.

value.en: Daughter of King Eylimi
A valkyrie who "rode air and sea"; she gave Helgi his name and often shielded him in battle
Telling Helgi of a sword at Sigarshólmr: a ring in the hilt, a blood-flecked snake along the edge
Helgi Hjörvarðsson; they loved each other greatly, but she stayed at home with her father and remained a valkyrie
When the dying Helgi asked her to love his brother Heðinn, she refused an unknown man. A later prose note says Sigrún was Sváfa born again

why.en: She tells the silent prince where the best of fifty-four swords lies.
Her vow: never to hold an unknown prince in her arms after Helgi.

hook.en: Sigurðr's daughter, brighter than the sun, trampled to death under horses after a courtier betrayed her to the king.

value.en: Daughter of Sigurðr and Guðrún
Brought up at King Jónakr's court, after Guðrún married him; "of all women she was fairest"
Sent to marry the old King Jörmunrekkr. Earl Bikki said the king's young son Randvér should have her instead, then reported this to the king
Jörmunrekkr's riders trod her under their horses' feet as she sat washing her hair

why.en: Brynhildr foretells her: whiter than the bright day.
Guðrún: she was like a ray of the sun in my hall.
Guðrún's charge to her sons: your sister was trampled.

hook.en: The black-elves' land, where dwarfs made the fetter Gleipnir and Loki robbed the dwarf Andvari of his gold.

value.en: Snorri's name for the land of the black-elves, where dwarfs live
Allfather sent Skírnir down there to have dwarfs make the fetter Gleipnir
Óðinn sent Loki there; he caught the dwarf Andvari and took all his gold and his ring

why.en: The six impossible things that make Gleipnir.
Loki robs Andvari, and the ring is cursed.

hook.en: One of the two he-goats that pull Þórr's chariot, slaughtered for supper and raised again with his hammer.

value.en: One of Þórr's two he-goats (“Tooth-Gnasher”); the other is Tanngrisnir. They draw his chariot, which is why he is called Öku-Þórr
On a journey Þórr killed and cooked his goats, then hallowed the hides with Mjöllnir and they stood up again, one lame in a hind leg. Snorri does not say which
Snorri blames the farmer's son Þjálfi, who split a thigh-bone for the marrow; Hymiskviða blames Loki
In payment Þórr took the farmer's two children, Þjálfi and Röskva, as his servants

why.en: Þórr's goats, chariot and three treasures.
The goat supper and the broken thigh-bone.
Hymiskviða's version: Loki lamed the goat.

hook.en: Þórr's second he-goat, “Tooth-Gritter”; with Tanngnjóstr he pulls the chariot that gives Þórr the name Öku-Þórr.

value.en: One of the two he-goats that draw Þórr's chariot; the other is Tanngnjóstr
Þórr killed and cooked his goats at a farmer's house and raised them next morning with Mjöllnir; one rose lame
Hymiskviða says the goat lay half-dead and lame, and that Loki caused it

why.en: The goats and the name Öku-Þórr.
Supper, bones and resurrection at the farmer's house.

hook.en: A farmer's son who cracked a goat's bone for the marrow — and so became Þórr's servant for life.

value.en: Son of a farmer; brother of Röskva.
At supper he splits a thigh-bone of Þórr's goat for the marrow; the goat rises lame. The terrified farmer gives Þjálfi and Röskva to Þórr in compensation, and they follow him ever after.
The fastest runner of all men; he carries Þórr's bag. At Útgarðr he loses three races to Hugi, who was Útgarða-Loki's thought.
Against Hrungnir he tricks the giant into standing on his shield, and kills the clay giant Mökkurkálfi.
Poets call Þórr "Master of Thjálfi and Röskva".

why.en: How a broken bone bought a servant.
The first race against Hugi.
Þjálfi's trick on Hrungnir.

hook.en: A giant who, in eagle shape, forced Loki to lure Iðunn out of Ásgarðr — and died with his feathers on fire.

value.en: Son of Ölvaldi; brothers Iði and Gangr; father of Skaði. In Hárbarðsljóð he is "Alvaldi's son".
Þrymheimr, in the mountains; after his death his daughter Skaði lives there.
As an eagle he spoils the gods' meal, drags Loki through the rocks on a stuck pole, and frees him only on an oath to bring out Iðunn and her apples. Then he carries her off.
He chases Loki, who flies home as a falcon with Iðunn; the gods light wood shavings, his feathers catch fire, and the Æsir kill him inside the gate.
His eyes become two stars. Snorri says Óðinn threw them up; in Hárbarðsljóð Þórr claims both the killing and the stars; in Lokasenna Loki says he was first at the kill.
He and his brothers shared their father's gold by mouthfuls, so poets call gold the giants' "speech".

why.en: Loki dangling from an eagle's back.
The chase over the wall of Ásgarðr.
Þórr's own boast about Þjazi's eyes.
Why gold is "the speech of giants".

hook.en: The one giantess who would not weep Baldr out of Hel — only "waterless tears" — and many think she was Loki.

value.en: A cave, where the gods' messengers find her on their way home.
Everything in the world weeps for Baldr except her. She says she will weep "waterless tears": "Let Hel hold to that she hath!"
Snorri says people think she was Loki, who had done most harm among the Æsir.

why.en: The whole world weeps for Baldr.
Þökk's short, cold verse.
Who people say she really was.

hook.en: The strongest of gods and men, whose raised hammer the giants know too well. The World Serpent's venom kills him.

value.en: Son of Óðinn and Jörð (Earth). Husband of Sif, father of Magni, Móði and Þrúðr, stepfather of Ullr.
The hall Bilskirnir, with 540 rooms, the biggest house known, in the realm of Þrúðvangar. Grímnismál calls his land Þrúðheimr.

The hammer Mjöllnir; a belt of strength that adds half again to his strength; and iron gloves he needs to grip the hammer's shaft. Forged by the dwarf Sindri, the hammer never misses and always returns to his hand, but its handle is rather short.
A chariot drawn by two goats, Tanngnjóstr and Tanngrisnir. That is why he is called Öku-Þórr, driving Þórr.
Fighting giants. He defends Ásgarðr and Miðgarðr, and has killed Hrungnir, Geirröðr, the wall-builder and Þrymr.
At Ragnarök he kills the Miðgarðr serpent, walks nine steps, and falls dead from its venom. His sons Móði and Magni inherit Mjöllnir.

why.en: His goats, his hammer, his belt and his iron gloves.
Þórr wakes up and finds his hammer gone.
Þórr hauls the serpent up to the boat's side and strikes it.
How the dwarfs made Mjöllnir, and its one flaw.
Ragnarök: Þórr and the serpent kill each other.

hook.en: Þórr's daughter, known almost only from poets' phrases — one of which hints that Hrungnir stole her.

value.en: Daughter of Þórr and Sif
Poets call Þórr Þrúðr's father
Bragi calls Hrungnir's shield the sole-blade of Þrúðr's thief, hinting at a lost story in which the giant carried her off
A valkyrie who carries ale in Valhöll has the same name; nothing links the two

why.en: Bragi's riddling line about Þrúðr's thief.
Þórr, as Þrúðr's father, glares at the serpent.

hook.en: Þórr's own realm, where he goes home after his adventures — once with a piece of whetstone stuck in his head.

value.en: Þórr's realm (ríki); his hall Bilskirnir stands there
Þórr comes home there after Útgarða-Loki's tricks, and after the fight with Hrungnir, with the whetstone in his head; the seeress Gróa sang over him there
In Grímnismál Þórr's land is called Þrúðheimr

why.en: Gróa's spells, and why you should not throw a whetstone.
Þórr turns back home to Þrúðvangar.

hook.en: Mountain home of the giant Þjazi, then of his daughter Skaði, who skis and hunts there.

value.en: In the mountains; once the home of the giant Þjazi
Skaði, Þjazi's daughter; she goes on skis with a bow and shoots game
Þjazi carried Iðunn off there in eagle shape
Her husband Njörðr found the mountains hateful after nine nights: the wolves' howling was ugly beside the song of swans

why.en: Njörðr's verse against the mountains.
Skaði in her father's old home.

hook.en: Lord of the giants, who hid Þórr's hammer and demanded Freyja as ransom — and got Þórr in a bridal veil.

value.en: Called þursa dróttinn, "the giants' master". He sits on a mound twisting golden leashes for his dogs and smoothing his horses' manes.
He hides Þórr's hammer eight leagues under the earth and will return it only for Freyja as his wife.
He is rich: gold-horned cows, all-black oxen, many treasures — he lacks only Freyja.
He marvels at a bride who eats so much and has such burning eyes; Loki, as her maid, explains it away.
He has the hammer laid in the bride's lap to bless the marriage. Þórr seizes it and kills him first, then all his kin.

why.en: The giant lord at home, grooming his dogs and horses.
The ransom demand.
Þrymr notices how his bride eats and drinks.
The hammer comes back to its owner.

hook.en: The boldest of the gods, who put his right hand in the wolf's mouth as a pledge — and lost it.

value.en: Courage and wisdom; he has great power over victory in battle. The bravest man is called "Týr-valiant".
His right hand, bitten off by Fenrir when the gods bound the wolf
Óðinn, in Snorri; in Hymiskviða Týr calls the giant Hymir his father
At Ragnarök he fights the hound Garmr; each kills the other

why.en: The binding of Fenrir: only Týr dares, and only Týr does not laugh.
Loki mocks him for his lost hand; Týr's answer follows.
Týr tells Þórr that his giant father Hymir owns a huge kettle.

hook.en: A god of bow and skis, Sif's son and Þórr's stepson, by whose ring oaths were once sworn.

value.en: Son of Sif and stepson of Þórr
No one can match him with the bow or on skis. He is handsome and has a warrior's skills; it is good to call on him in single combat.
God of the snowshoe, god of the bow, hunting god, shield god
Ýdalir, where he has built himself a hall
In Grímnismál the tormented Óðinn promises "the favor of Ull" to whoever first reaches into the fire for him; in Atlakviða oaths are sworn by "the ring of Ull"

why.en: Everything Snorri says about him, in four sentences.
Óðinn, caught between fires, promises Ullr's favour to a rescuer.
Guðrún reminds Atli of oaths sworn on Ullr's ring.
His hall at Ýdalir, in Óðinn's list of the gods' homes.

hook.en: The holy well under heaven's root of the world-ash, where the gods hold court and the Norns live.

value.en: A very holy well under the root of Yggdrasill that stands in heaven; the gods have their court there
Three maidens, Urðr, Verðandi and Skuld, in a hall by the well; they shape men's lives and are called Norns
Every day the Norns pour its water and the white clay round it over the ash; whatever enters it turns white as the skin inside an eggshell
Two swans feed in it, ancestors of all swans
The gods ride to it every day over Bifröst; Þórr walks and wades the rivers

why.en: The ash stands ever green over Urðr's well.
The chanter of Hávamál says he was "By the wells of Urth".
The Norns tend the tree with the well's water.

hook.en: A giant king who beat Þórr and his companions at every contest — through illusions — and then explained how.

value.en: King of the stronghold Útgarðr. He is not the god Loki, who comes as one of Þórr's party and competes against his household.
His contests: Loki against Logi in eating, Þjálfi against Hugi in running, Þórr at draining a horn, lifting a cat and wrestling an old woman.
He reveals the tricks: he was the giant in the forest; Logi was wildfire, Hugi his own thought; the horn reached the sea; the cat was the Miðgarðr serpent; the old woman was old age.
Calls the old woman Elli (Old Age) his foster-mother.
When Þórr raises his hammer, the king and his stronghold vanish, leaving open plains.

why.en: The giant king sneers at Þórr as "this toddler".
The truth behind each contest.
What Þórr really lifted and wrestled.
The castle disappears.

hook.en: A giant known as the wisest of all, who wagered his head against Óðinn in a contest of knowledge — and lost.

value.en: Called the all-wise giant (inn alsvinni jötunn). Frigg tells Óðinn she knows no giant as strong as him.
Óðinn visits him as Gagnráðr. They sit together and wager their heads on who knows more.
He knows the oldest lore: the world made from Ymir, Bergelmir's birth, how the giants came from Élivágar. He says he has been to nine worlds, down to Niflhel.
He also knows the future: who survives the great winter, and who rules after Surtr's fire.
Óðinn asks what he whispered to his dead son. Vafþrúðnir sees who his guest is, says he has spoken "with fated mouth", and names Óðinn the wisest.
Called "father of Ímr".

why.en: Frigg warns Óðinn: no giant is his match.
The stakes are set: their heads.
His own earliest memory: Bergelmir laid on a lúðr.
The giant recognises Óðinn and admits defeat.

hook.en: Óðinn's hall of the battle-dead: spears for rafters, shields for its roof, and 540 doors.

value.en: Óðinn's wide, gold-bright hall in Glaðsheimr; there he chooses each day the men killed by weapons. Its rafters are spears, its roof shields
The einherjar: men fallen in battle, "the sons of his adoption" (Óðinn's); valkyries serve them drink
Meat from the boar Sæhrímnir, boiled every day and whole again by evening; mead from the goat Heiðrún, who eats from the tree Læraðr
540 doors; 800 warriors go out of each at once when they go to fight the wolf
Every day the warriors arm, fight and fell each other, then ride home to drink
Not every fallen fighter goes there: Freyja chooses half the slain each day for Fólkvangr; those dead of sickness or old age go to Hel

why.en: A wolf hangs by the west door; an eagle hovers above.
540 doors, 800 men through each.
Helgi comes to Valhöll; Óðinn offers him rule over everything with himself.

hook.en: Born to avenge Baldr: one night old, hands unwashed and hair uncombed, he killed Baldr's slayer.

value.en: Áli or Váli, daring in battle and a lucky shot
Son of Óðinn and Rindr; stepson of Frigg
Avenging Baldr by killing Höðr
In Baldrs draumar the seeress foretells that Rindr will bear him in Vestrsalir; one night old he will fight, and will not wash his hands or comb his hair until Baldr's slayer is on the pyre
Völuspá tells the same of an unnamed "brother of Baldr", a son of Óðinn, who fights when one night old
He survives Ragnarök and lives with Víðarr in the gods' home

why.en: The seeress foretells his birth and his revenge.
A short verse sums up the revenge for Baldr.
Völuspá: "the brother of Baldr", one night old, takes up the fight.
Váli and Víðarr will hold the gods' home after the fire.

hook.en: Loki's son, whose end is told two ways: turned into a wolf to kill his brother, or killed to bind his father.

value.en: Son of Loki; brother of Narfi (or Nari). His mother is not named
Áli: Skáldskaparmál lists an Áli among Loki's children, probably this son. The same names, Áli or Váli, belong to Óðinn's son by Rindr, a different figure
Snorri: after Baldr's death the gods turn Váli into a wolf, he tears his brother Narfi apart, and Loki is bound with Narfi's guts
The prose at the end of Lokasenna turns it round: Loki is bound with Váli's guts, and Narfi becomes a wolf
Lines in the Hauksbók Völuspá say Váli twisted slaughter-bonds, fetters made of guts; they do not say which Váli

why.en: Snorri's version: Váli the wolf, and the binding of Loki.
Lokasenna's closing prose: Váli's guts bind his father.
Skaði foretells the binding with the guts of Loki's son.

hook.en: The home of the Vanir, where Njörðr was raised — and, one poem says, where he will return when the world ends.

value.en: The land of the Vanir. Njörðr was brought up there and given to the gods as a hostage, in exchange for Hœnir
The Vanir, the "Wanes so wise" of Vafþrúðnismál
Vafþrúðnismál: "at the fall of the world" Njörðr will go home to the wise Vanir

why.en: The only poem to name Vanaheimr.
Njörðr, hostage between Vanir and Æsir.

hook.en: Óðinn's little-known brother, one of three who killed Ymir, made the world, and gave the first humans life.

value.en: Son of Borr and Bestla; brother of Óðinn and Vili.
With his brothers he kills Ymir and makes the world from his body.
The three brothers shape Askr and Embla from two trees and give them life, wits and senses. Snorri does not say which gift came from which brother.
In Lokasenna Loki taunts Frigg that she once took both Vé and Vili into her embrace.

why.en: Vé's birth, and Hárr's claim that the brothers rule heaven and earth.
The making of the first humans.
Loki's insult that drags Vé's name into the hall.

hook.en: The second of three norns who come from a hall by the well under the world-tree and set men's lives.

value.en: One of the three norns, Urðr, Verðandi and Skuld
A hall under the ash Yggdrasill, by Urðr's well
"Laws they made there, and life allotted to the sons of men"; "On the wood they scored". Snorri: they decide the length of men's lives.
There are many other norns, who come to each child at birth: some of the gods' kin, some of the elves', some of the dwarves'. Good norns shape good lives; bad lives come from evil norns.

why.en: The seeress names the three norns.
Snorri on the three norns and the many others.
Why lives are so unequal: good and evil norns.

hook.en: One of four dwarves set under the corners of the sky; his name means simply "West".

value.en: One of four dwarves the gods set under the four corners of the sky: Austri, Vestri, Norðri, Suðri (East, West, North, South)
Under a corner of the sky, which the gods made from the skull of the giant Ymir
Poets may call the sky the "helm" of Vestri, Austri, Suðri and Norðri, or the "task" or "burden" of the dwarves
The name also stands in Völuspá's list of dwarves

why.en: The gods build the sky from Ymir's skull.
How poets name the sky after the four dwarves.

hook.en: The silent god who avenges Óðinn on the wolf at Ragnarök, in a shoe made of leather scraps men trim away.

value.en: The silent god. He is almost as strong as Þórr, and the gods rely on him in every struggle.
Son of Óðinn and the giantess Gríðr
Viði, a land overgrown with brushwood and tall grass
A thick shoe, made of the scraps men cut from their shoes at toe and heel; Snorri also calls it an iron shoe
Killing Fenrir after the wolf swallows Óðinn. Snorri: he sets his shod foot on the lower jaw and tears the jaws apart. Völuspá: he drives his sword into its heart. Vafþrúðnismál: he splits its jaws.
He survives the sea and Surtr's fire and lives with Váli at Iðavöllr, where Ásgarðr used to be

why.en: Ragnarök: Óðinn falls, and Víðarr's shoe finds its purpose.
The older poem's version: a sword to the wolf's heart.
His land of tall grass, where he leaps from his horse to avenge his father.
Óðinn tells him to stand and give the wolf's father a seat.
His mother Gríðr lends Þórr her belt, gloves and staff.

hook.en: The battlefield of Ragnarök: a hundred leagues wide in every direction.

value.en: The field where Surtr and the gods will meet in battle; a hundred rastir (leagues) each way
Múspell's sons, the wolf Fenrir, the Miðgarðsormr, Loki, Hrymr and all the frost-giants gather there
Fáfnismál gives the gods' last battle-place a different name: the island Óskópnir

why.en: Óðinn names the field in his contest with a giant.
Who comes to Vígríðr.

hook.en: A fair hall of the goddesses on Iðavöllr — and, Snorri also says, a home for the good and the battle-dead.

value.en: A sanctuary (hörgr) belonging to the goddesses, "a very fair house"
On Iðavöllr in Ásgarðr, built after Glaðsheimr
Snorri also says that righteous people will live with Allfather in Gimlé or Vingólf (the English translation leaves Vingólf out), and that Óðinn appoints Valhöll and Vingólf for the battle-slain

why.en: The gods' first buildings: Glaðsheimr, then Vingólf.
Óðinn gives the slain Valhöll and Vingólf.

hook.en: A master smith, lamed and imprisoned by a king, who took a terrible revenge and rose into the air laughing.

value.en: Völundr, son of a king of the Finns, brother of Slagfiðr and Egill; "a most skillful man, as men know from old tales". The poem calls him "greatest of elves" and "master of elves".
Hervör the all-wise, a valkyrie in swan's garb, daughter of King Hlöðvér. After seven winters she flew away and did not come back.
His freedom: King Níðuðr took him asleep, kept his sword and gave one of his rings to Böðvildr. On the queen's advice his knee sinews were cut and he was set to forge on an island.
His revenge: he killed the king's two sons, set their skulls in silver for the king, made gems of their eyes for the queen and a brooch of their teeth for Böðvildr, and left Böðvildr pregnant
"Laughing Völund rose aloft", out of anyone's reach; the poem does not say how he flew

why.en: The swan-maidens arrive and leave: how the story starts.
The revenge begins in the smithy.
Völundr escapes into the air; Níðuðr is left behind.

hook.en: The world's ash: the gods meet at it daily while a dragon gnaws its root and harts eat its shoots.

value.en: An ash, "greatest of all trees and best"; its branches spread over the whole world and stand above heaven

Three roots. Snorri puts them among the Æsir (over Urðarbrunnr, in heaven), among the frost-giants (over Mímisbrunnr) and over Niflheimr (over Hvergelmir). Grímnismál: Hel lives under one, frost-giants under another, men under the third
An eagle with the hawk Veðrfölnir between its eyes; the squirrel Ratatoskr carrying words between the eagle and Níðhöggr; four harts; countless serpents
It suffers: the hart bites above, the trunk rots, Níðhöggr gnaws below. The Norns pour water and white clay from Urðr's well over it so it will not wither
The gods hold court at the tree every day; Þórr wades rivers to get there
At Ragnarök the ash trembles and the old tree groans as the giant breaks loose

why.en: The tree in Völuspá: ever green over Urðr's well.
"Yggdrasil's ash great evil suffers."
Snorri's tour of the creatures in the tree.

hook.en: The first being: a giant who grew out of melting rime, was killed by Óðinn and his brothers, and became the world.

value.en: The first giant, quickened from drops where the rime met the heat from Múspell. All giants come from him; Snorri's Hárr says he was evil and no god.
The frost giants call him Aurgelmir. In Vafþrúðnismál Aurgelmir is Bergelmir's grandfather.
While he slept, a man and a woman grew under his left arm, and one foot begot a son with the other; in Vafþrúðnismál that son has six heads.
Fed by four rivers of milk from the cow Auðhumla.
Killed by the sons of Borr. His blood drowned all the frost giants except Bergelmir, who escaped with his wife and household.
The world is made from his body: earth from flesh, sea from blood, rocks from bones, sky from skull, clouds from brain, the wall of Miðgarðr from his brows.

why.en: How the first living thing woke in the void.
His death, and the flood of blood that drowned his kin.
The world built from his body, in verse.
A giant's own account of how Ymir had children.
